title: Hanson apologises if she caused offence by Indigenous Australian remarks
text:
One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has offered qualified apologies for labelling Indigenous Australians "the most primitive race on Earth" and criticising the prime minister's late mother.

Senator Hanson faced widespread condemnation on Monday after the remarks from conservative-leaning Jamie J podcast came to light, where she criticised the amount of focus on Indigenous history in the school curriculum.

"Sorry they're the most primitive race on Earth and we're supposed to be holding them up and saying what they've achieved. They've achieved nothing," she said last September.

Politicians from across the divide swiftly rebuked the comments, among them Indigenous Australians Minister Malarndirri McCarthy, who said they were "derogatory" and "completely racist" and urged her to apologise.

Hanson Indigenous comments widely condemned Politicians from across the divide have condemned Pauline Hanson's remarks about Indigenous Australians, labelling them "vile", "divisive" and "derogatory".

In her first public remarks since, Senator Hanson said she did not mean to cause offence by the comments.

"If I've offended people by using that, yes, I will apologise for that," she told reporters.

"I've always advocated, we are Australians all together and should be all treated equally on a needs basis, not about race. And until we actually do that, we're not going to move over what's happened in the past."

On Monday, several Indigenous leaders expressed their "disappointment" over the "primitive" label, calling Senator Hanson's claims not only "false" but demonstrating ignorance.

Indigenous author and human rights activist Thomas Mayo was among them, arguing that that Senator Hanson's view is not shared by Australians.

"Many Australians have learnt that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples built sophisticated systems of law, governance, culture, trade, and land management over tens of thousands of years," he said.

"We have survived invasion, dispossession and every attempt to erase us. We are still here and will always remain in the rich tapestry of Australian identity."

Speaking to News24 earlier today, Senator Hanson claimed "[I] put my foot in my mouth" and that the comments about First Nations people were referring to the past, when Australia was colonised.

"If we go back at the time of settlement in Australia, they were primitive compared to what the settlers that came out here from England, that type of thing. But I'm not talking those terms now. It's not about now," Senator Hanson said.

"I regret saying that because I don't want to upset people. That's not my intentions. That wasn't my intention to hurt people."

Calls for Hanson to apologise to PM

Senator Hanson was also asked if she regretted saying it was "not on" for Anthony Albanese's mother Maryanne, who suffered from severe rheumatoid arthritis, to have spent much of her life in housing commission.

"I don't think my comments were derogatory towards his mother at all. I was referring to house commission at that time. So if he's taken offence to it, well, I'm sorry for that," she said.

The criticism of Mr Albanese's late mother, who died in 2002, prompted calls from several politicians for Senator Hanson to apologise to the prime minister.

Mr Albanese has been open about his upbringing in public housing in Sydney's inner west, repeated references that Senator Hanson labelled "pathetic" on a podcast with Karl Stefanovic earlier this year.

"I actually grew up in a street where we had housing commission houses there. It was a helping hand to those people, but they had jobs. And they worked," she told Stefanovic.

PM defends late mother Anthony Albanese has fiercely defended his late mother against criticism by Pauline Hanson, who has been called on to apologise for her remarks.

"Housing commission houses should not be there for people to live in them for 30, 40 [years] — and he said his mother lived in the same one she was born in for 65 years."

In a fierce defence of his mother on Sunday morning, Mr Albanese said he was "stunned" by the attack, recalling a woman of "great character".

"If Pauline Hanson wants to criticise me, then that's fine, but my mother was way out of Pauline Hanson's league, way out of it," he said.

title: Emmys 2026 key moments: Widow's Bay takes six awards and Hacks star makes history
text:
The 78th Primetime Emmy Awards are over for another year, and there was a clear winner.

Widow's Bay, described as "weird" by the show's creator, dominated most categories it was nominated for, taking six awards home, while another frontrunner, The Pitt, only picked up two.

Here are the key moments from the ceremony.

Widow's Bay sweeps categories

Widow's Bay star Matthew Rhys makes history with his Emmy's win. (Getty Images: Rich Polk)

Matthew Rhys, who plays a New England mayor trying to boost tourism on his supposedly cursed island of Widow's Bay, made Emmy history.

Rhys is the first man to win two lead acting categories in the same year, after taking home the award for Lead Actor in a Limited or Anthology Series for The Beast in Me and Lead Comedy Actor in Widow's Bay.

"This is purely because of the depraved and twisted mind of Katie Dippold and my hero Hiro Murai," Rhys said when accepting the award for Widow's Bay.

"We had the crew of all crews.

"To the great people of Wales, who were as much a nurturer as anything else, we are a small but mighty nation."

The Welsh actor's partner Keri Russell, who was nominated for The Diplomat, was in the audience cheering and clapping in support.

Mayor Tom (Matthew Rhys, left) initially refuses to hear Wyck's (Stephen Root, right) warnings. (Supplied: AppleTV)

Japanese filmmaker Hiro Murai went on to take out Outstanding Directing for a Comedy Series for Widow's Bay.

Creator and showrunner Katie Dippold also picked up an Emmy for Best Comedy Writing for the show.

Widow's Bay won the first award of the ceremony when Kate O'Flynn took out Supporting Actress in a Comedy Series for her brilliant depiction of the awkward but loyal mayoral assistant Patricia.

"This is the role of a lifetime," O'Flynn said.

Widow's Bay continued its winning streak with Stephen Root winning Best Supporting Actor.

Root acknowledged his fellow nominees, who included Colman Domingo, Paul W Downs, Harrison Ford, Nick Offerman, Michael Urie and Tyler James Williams.

"You are all unbelievable. I am a huge fan," Root said.

"Thank you, Harrison Ford, because my son came running up to me and said, 'You're in a category with Harrison Ford!' Thank you, sir, for your many years of great, great, great, great acting."

The debut season of the Apple TV horror comedy also won eight Creative Arts Emmys.

Rhea Seehorn wins her first Emmy

Rhea Seehorn expressed shock when she won Outstanding Lead Actress in a Drama Series for her role in Pluribus as Carol, the most miserable person on Earth who must save the world from happiness.

Rhea Seehorn called Pluribus "the role of a lifetime". (Getty Images: Kevin Winter)

It was Seehorn's first Emmy.

She had been nominated three times at previous ceremonies, including twice for the Breaking Bad prequel Better Call Saul, and was a hot favourite to take out the award this year.

In an emotional speech, Seehorn thanked the members of the television academy who voted for her.

She went on to thank her fellow nominees.

Carol (Rhea Seehorn) is one of the only free-thinking people left on Earth in Pluribus. (Supplied: Apple TV+)

"All brilliant, brilliant performances," Seehorn said.

"Keri Russell, among them, sent a gift and a card quoting — I didn't know we were going to lose her so soon — Gloria Steinem saying, 'We are linked not ranked', and I feel that way about all you women, so thank you for that."

Vince Gilligan went on to win the Emmy for Writing for a Drama Series for Pluribus.

Gilligan and Seehorn worked together on Better Call Saul, which was nominated for 53 Emmys, but won zero.

Gilligan was also the creator, showrunner and executive producer of Breaking Bad.

He said in his speech there was nothing weirder than "our current reality".

"We will never agree on everything," he said.

"But we can show respect to one another, maybe even kindness, and we can stop listening to a relative few who tell us that that is for suckers and who get their power from dividing us."

Law and Order jokes and Taylor Swift cameo in Mariska Hargitay's hosting

Mariska Hargitay opened the show with a parody of I Love Rock N Roll dedicated to her love of television. (Getty Images: Chloe Kern)

The 2026 Emmys began with host Mariska Hargitay singing a cringeworthy interpolation of I Love Rock 'n' Roll, swapping out the words in the chorus and replacing them with "I love TV screens".

It wasn't the only time during the ceremony she broke out in song.

Emmys 2026 winners' list The 78th Primetime Emmy Awards has kicked off. Here is a list of the 2026 nominees and winners.

The Law & Order: SVU star, who plays Captain Olivia Benson on the long-running show, pointed out in her opening monologue that it had been 15 years since a woman had hosted the awards show.

"Imagine that, for 15 years Amy and Tina said no," she joked.

Hargitay went on to say she had arrested many of the actors in the crowd on SUV.

At one point during her monologue, Hargitay was interrupted by Australian superstar Nicole Kidman, who told her she was reading out her line.

"Zip it, movie lady," Hargitay replied.

"It's TV's turn tonight."

Later in the ceremony, pop star Taylor Swift made an appearance in a Law & Order skit playing a character that was not her, but one contemplating whether Swift would make an appearance at the Emmys.

It was established that she wouldn't be doing so, except in the skit (as someone else).

The two have often popped up in each other's work, with one of Swift's cats named after Hargitay's character Olivia Benson and the SVU star appearing in Swift's Bad Blood music video.

Jean Smart breaks record with lead actress win

Jean Smart keeps the speech for her eigth Emmy win short and sweet. (Getty Images: Chloe Kern)

Jean Smart's Best Leading Actress in a Comedy win makes her the first actress in Emmy's history to take the award for every season of their show.

Smart's show Hacks finished with its fifth season earlier this year, in which she played comedian Deborah Vance, who teams up with a zillennial comedy writer to revamp her career.

Jean Smart is now also tied with Cloris Leachman, Allison Janney and Julia Louis Dreyfus for the most acting wins in prime-time Emmy history, with eight wins in total.

Allison Janney also reached eight wins tonight for her work on The Diplomat.

Julia Louis-Dreyfus came very close with her six consecutive wins for Veep, but was beaten in 2019 when Phoebe Waller-Bridge won for season two of Fleabag.

Hannah Einbinder as Ava Daniels and Jean Smart as Deborah Vance in Hacks. (Supplied: Stan)

Smart now has five Emmys for Hacks and three for her work on Frasier, Designing Women and Samantha Who.

Smart dedicated the award to Hacks creators Lucia Aniello, Paul W Downs and Jen Statsky.

Her speech was short and sharp, telling all the ladies in the audience to sit.

"Just the men stay standing, the girls get to sit down," she said.

"We just stood up because she's old," she joked.

Stephen Colbert wins Emmy for final season, thanks writers

Stephen Colbert has taken home an Emmy for Best Late Night Show after he was pulled from the air this year.

The Late Show with Stephen Colbert wrapped up for good in May, bringing an end to a late-night franchise that has occupied New York's historic Ed Sullivan Theatre since the early 1990s.

Stephen Colbert shouts out writers. (Getty Images: Los Angeles Times)

CBS executives released a statement calling the move a "purely financial decision", labelling Colbert "irreplaceable".

The announcement came in the middle of last year, as Paramount was seeking approval from the Federal Communications Commission for a merger with Skydance to create one of the largest entertainment companies in American history.

Colbert, a fervent critic of President Donald Trump, had also just days earlier castigated CBS for settling a lawsuit filed by Trump against 60 Minutes for $US16 million, despite many legal experts believing the case had little chance of success (Colbert called the settlement a "big fat bribe").

But Colbert didn't talk about that.

Can late-night talk shows survive Trump? With Stephen Colbert's Late Show wrapping up this week, the future of late-night talk — an American cultural institution — has never looked more perilous.

Instead, he chose to use the win to shout-out his writers, who are now looking for work.

"I just want to point out that if you like the comedy tonight, my old writer wrote it," he opened his speech.

"Thank you so much on behalf of the over 200 people who threw themselves at this show for 11 years to try to do the best show they could for you.

"Hire them. They will make your show better, and they will make your day easier."

Colbert joked he had interviewed "thousands" of people in the room over the years, but said his wife Evelyn was his favourite guest.

"Well, catch you all on the flip," he signed off.

Tributes flow for Dolly Parton, Catherine O'Hara and more

The entertainment industry has lost many actors, musicians and artists in the past 12 months, with a significant portion of the night dedicated to them.

First up was a rendition of Appalachian Memories performed by Reba McEntire in tribute to Dolly Parton, who died in August.

Her Steel Magnolias co-star Sally Field offered kind words about Parton's unique character.

"If there are truly angels on Earth, then we just lost one," she starts.

"I am not the only one on Earth who will love you forever and forever."

The in memoriam portion of the evening began with Catherine O'Hara's co-stars Macaulay Culkin from Home Alone and Annie Murphy and Dan Levy from Schitt's Creek.

Catherine O'Hara is paid tribute to by her co-stars. (Getty Images: Rich Polk)

Annie Murphy spoke of how she had been approached by fans since O'Hara's death in January.

Dan Levy shared that the greatest lesson he learnt from O'Hara was to "say yes".

"Say yes to the concept of a wig wall," he said.

"Say yes to her wearing a wig as a hat.

"Say yes to her naming that wig."

Jamie Lee Curtis then took to the stage to speak about the loss of Frasier and Will and Grace director James Burrows, and filmmaker and actor Rob Reiner.

Jamie Lee Curtis gets emotional when she talks about Rob Reiner. (Getty Images: Rich Polk)

"Last week, Robby won an Emmy for his work on The Bear and now he holds the record for longest gap between Emmys, which was previously held by his father Carl Reiner.

"He was generous and funny and kind, and we miss Rob and Michelle."

title: Whyalla's steelmaking gap could last years as potential job losses mount
text:
A resumption of steelmaking in Whyalla could be several years away, following the announcement that its ailing blast furnace will not be restarted.

About 500 workers at the South Australian regional city's steelworks will lose their jobs, along with 100 labour hire workers, administrators KordaMentha revealed on Monday.

The future is unclear for another 200 "embedded contractors" employed by external companies to work at the steelworks, potentially taking the total number of initial job losses to about 800.

"That's probably a fair number but it's hard to say," KordaMentha partner Sebastian Hams said on Monday.

SA Premier Peter Malinauskas said it was necessary to "exercise a degree of caution" around that figure, because some of the contractors had work elsewhere.

"There's a bit of speculation about that, as I understand it, but it's impossible to know just at this point because, obviously, contractors who provide services on the site will make their own decisions," he said on Tuesday.

The job losses have been precipitated by the demise of the steelworks' 60-year-old blast furnace — a critical piece of infrastructure that made pig iron, which was then converted into steel.

Whyalla's steelworks is the only Australian manufacturer of long steel products. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

While the furnace has been offline since April, its long-term problems date back at least several years and KordaMentha said it was no longer feasible to attempt to restart it.

"The blast furnace will now go completely cold — we can't do what's called a 'controlled blow-down' because we literally can't get enough air into it," Mr Hams said.

Estimates have varied for how long it will take for a future owner of the steelworks to replace the coal-fired furnace with a long-proposed electric arc furnace — a technology that uses plasma to melt scrap.

Mayor Phill Stone said that, despite the blast furnace's age, the end to its life cycle had been more abrupt than anticipated.

"We always knew there was going to be a new chapter — we didn't expect it quite so soon," he told ABC News Breakfast.

"We'll now have that period between the new buyers being selected, the new technology coming online in a few years' time, but have to get through this immediate period where we will have job losses."

Mayor Phill Stone says the resumption of steelmaking will take three to four years.

While the government yesterday announced various support measures for workers, Mr Stone said there were families who "may have to think about relocating" — but added that there were other opportunities in the region and South Australia's north more broadly, including with BHP.

"It is probably going to be a three-to-four-year process — we will still be rolling rail line steel," he said.

"It sounds ridiculous, but we will be bringing steel in so that the steel mill can continue."

Two bidders — Jindal Steel and M Resources — remain in the running to buy the steelworks, while BlueScope Steel retains its right of last offer.

Sale 'not an auction'

South Australian Treasurer Tom Koutsantonis said a return to steelmaking would depend "on who the successful bidder is".

"There was always going to be a gap, there was always going to be a time when the blast furnace closed — between then and the new construction of the new facilities — because both bidders weren't going to keep underwriting the loss the blast furnace was making," he told 891 ABC Adelaide.

"I think we will see steelmaking again in the next couple of years in Whyalla."

'No steelworks, no town': Whyalla's fight for a future While the steelmaking city of Whyalla is no stranger to struggle, the latest crisis is taking a severe toll on the population, who very much want to continue making steel for Australia but say they are "sick of having to be resilient".

Journalist and author Paul Barry — whose book The Big Steal details the unravelling of the business empire of former Whyalla steelworks owner Sanjeev Gupta — said he thought a two-year time frame was unlikely.

"I think it's going to be three years at least. That's my understanding," the former ABC Media Watch host said.

"The buyers who are being lined up for Whyalla — they had no desire to have the blast furnace because it loses money, and so it would add to the cost of any bailout and add to their cost of taking it over.

"But I think that within three years with luck Whyalla could have a new modern steelmaking facility that will last for years and years and years."

Barry estimated $500 million had been spent since the site was forced into administration in early 2025, and suggested that everything hinged on a sale being secured sooner rather than later.

"I don't want to cast doubt on the proceedings but it was supposed to happen by September and it's not happened so clearly something is proving difficult," he said.

"If the sale goes ahead in the next three months, I think Whyalla will have a future and I think it will make steel again."

Whyalla's steelworks are no stranger to turmoil. (ABC News: Brant Cumming)

Mr Koutsantonis said the state and federal governments had greater control of the situation than they did when the steelworks were last in the hands of administrators KordaMentha, prior to Mr Gupta taking over the site in 2017.

"The banks were the ones who ran the administration and they wanted the highest bidder," he said.

"[But] this isn't a contest of who will pay the most for the steelworks — this is a contest of who is most capable of operating the steelworks.

"We're doing a capability assessment, not an auction on who can pay us the most.

"What we're trying to do is recapitalise with government money to make sure we're never here again."

title: The moment this Knights finals rookie will hold onto forever
text:
Last Friday's semifinal win over South Sydney was one of the great nights in Newcastle's recent history, and nobody enjoyed it more than Jermaine McEwen.

In his first finals match, the 21-year-old had the game of his young life, inspiring the 20-10 upset victory that has the whole Hunter dreaming big ahead of Sunday's sudden-death clash with the Warriors.

McEwen scored the first double of his NRL career and ran for 187 metres, the best mark of his 37 first-grade matches, and set the tone for the Knights' right-edge defence with a physical brutality that would make a mafia kingpin proud.

Knights win is proof the future has come Stars were born under the finals lights as Newcastle knockout finals win over South Sydney announced the dawn of a new tomorrow.

On a night of many highlights, McEwen's personal favourite was his second try that helped Newcastle kick clear in the second half, as he backed up winger Dom Young to score right in front of the Knights faithful.

McEwen crawled the last few metres before slamming the ball down so hard it's a wonder they could dig it out of the turf.

"The only reason I slammed it was because my parents and my family were right in front of me. I just looked at them, and I was like, 'hell yeah,'" said McEwen.

"That was the best moment I have ever had in my footy career. That moment right there, that's something I will hold forever. So I am just super grateful and so happy."

McEwen's first try of the evening helped get things started as he again trailed Young after the Englishman claimed a bomb inside the first five minutes.

It brought Newcastle into the match and gave the team the start they needed en route to their first away finals win since 2013 and just their third since their last premiership 25 years ago.

Repeating the dose in Auckland is a tall order, but even before the win over Souths, McEwen and his teammates did not lack for belief.

"The Knights have given me everything, and I believe in the coach, Justin (Holbrook). He's allowed me to be the greatest version of myself on that field," said McEwen.

"But when I put the ball down and looked up and saw all the fans, I was (thinking) how happy I am to be a Knight. I'm just so grateful.

"We just wanted to go out there and play with energy and lift each other up."

Newcastle's right edge did a fine job shutting down South Sydney's attack. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

McEwen spent much of the week thinking about how the Knights would shut down South Sydney's left edge, which is just about the most dangerous attacking weapon in the NRL.

Between them, Alex Johnston, Latrell Mitchell, Tallis Duncan and Cody Walker scored 63 tries in 2026, two more than Newcastle managed as an entire club last season.

But McEwen, Sandon Smith and Dane Gagai rose to the occasion magnificently, locking onto the superstars and refusing to let go, moving and defending as one.

Souths did end up scoring down the left through Jye Grey, but only after McEwen had left the field late on.

"When you have challenges, you get more prepared for it. You think about it more. When you're at home or training, you get flashbacks of what you have to do," said McEwen.

"When I have Cody Walker and their left edge — they do it the best in the whole comp. Cody Walker, he is just so good at that stuff.

"Us in D, we had a big job to do, and we just went out there and did it."

Jermaine McEwen and the Knights will look to pull off another finals ambush this Sunday against the Warriors. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

The journey through this year to Sunday's knockout final has not always been smooth for McEwen.

He was suspended for one match in June after being charged with low-range drink driving, an incident for which he apologised unreservedly and left him "deeply ashamed".

At the time, McEwen said he let his community down, and he's been trying to make amends ever since.

"Bro, at the end of the day we're all human and just because I play footy doesn't mean I'm special," said McEwen.

"In those circumstances, with the rollercoaster (of this year), that has taught me a lot in life.

"I feel like people can either shy away from it or own up to it. I wanted to show up for the fans and show them what I could do, and repay them in that way."

"Because I know how much the town speaks to this club and the hold this club has on the town. I wanted to repay them with good footy."

A sellout crowd is expected at Eden Park on Sunday, and a win would send Newcastle to just its second preliminary final in the last 25 years.

They'll again be underdogs against a Warriors side that beat them just three weeks ago, and the match marks the biggest game of McEwen's career, as it is for several of his teammates.

But the same was true last Friday, and by leaning on the experience of men like Gagai and prop Tyson Frizell, McEwen was inspired to make a difference, and all he wants is to do it all over again.

"These are experienced boys who have been in the game for a lot of years, and when you have them talk to you, it makes you more comfortable," said McEwen.

"You're not nervous. You're going out there to do a good job."

title: Macklemore dropped from Ed Sheeran tour over pro-Palestinian comments
text:
American rapper Macklemore says he has been dropped from pop star Ed Sheeran's US tour after his pro-Palestinian comments during a September 4 concert at New Jersey's MetLife Stadium.

Macklemore, whose real name is Benjamin Haggerty, wrote on Instagram he and Sheeran had "some difficult conversations this past week".

Messina Touring Group, promoter of the US leg of Sheeran's Loop Tour, told Rolling Stone that venue owners on the upcoming US tour dates notified the promoters they would not allow a concert to take place with Macklemore in the line-up.

"After discussions with stakeholders, Macklemore will not be performing on the remaining support dates," Messina Touring Group said.

Sheeran had no immediate comment.

The Loop Tour is scheduled to resume on September 19 in Philadelphia. (AP: Andy Kropa/Invision/File)

"A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: 'Free Palestine,'" Macklemore said earlier this month.

"I want those words to be loud and clear, so that people all the way in Gaza, to the occupied West Bank know that we have not forgotten about them," Macklemore had said during the concert.

Macklemore, a Grammy-winning artist, was on the bill to perform at eight of the 10 shows Sheeran has left on his stadium tour, which will resume on September 19 in Philadelphia, according to Variety.

The Israeli-American Council started a petition urging Sheeran to remove Macklemore from the tour.

Macklemore said on Instagram that New England Patriots owner and billionaire Robert Kraft rallied support among some stadium owners and told Sheeran they would not allow him to perform at their venues if Macklemore stayed on the tour.

In a statement to US media, Mr Kraft said much of his time was dedicated to fighting hate and antisemitism and he felt "a responsibility to stand up when I believe that line has been crossed".

Macklemore denies being antisemitic and said that conflating antisemitism with criticism of Israel's actions aimed to avoid Israeli accountability.

Reuters

title: I'm childless not by choice, but I do have biological children
text:
People would often tell Brett he'd make a great dad.

"I'd always go, 'I appreciate that,"' the 49-year-old from NSW says. "But to know I couldn't … that did hurt."

After trying to have a baby for many years, Brett (not his real name) and his wife were told by a fertility specialist they would be unlikely to conceive naturally. The couple decided not to pursue IVF.

Brett had been considering becoming a sperm donor. But, fearing it would upset his wife, he never shared his desire.

Then, after learning his cousin used an egg donor to get pregnant, it was his wife who suggested he consider donating.

"I nearly fell over," Brett says.

We spoke with Brett about how assisting others with infertility has helped his own grief with childlessness.

These are his words.

Kids weren't going to happen for us

We'd tried on and off over the years to get pregnant.

The grief of childlessness on Father's Day Michael Hughes had always imagined being a dad, but it didn't eventuate for him. Father's Day is especially painful, as it was the day his wife had a miscarriage almost two decades ago.

When we went to a fertility clinic, they did some tests and said it would take a lot of IVF and even then, may not be successful.

My wife also went through early menopause. So that put a full stop on the biological aspect.

I love my wife very much and she loves me, and we always thought we'd like to have a little one of us at home to grow and nurture.

It was a very sad thing to know that wasn't going to happen for us.

I'd had the thought about donating for years. But knowing that my wife couldn't get pregnant, I thought it would be unfair of me to mention that.

Then my cousin fell pregnant with a donor egg and my wife said, "I wouldn't mind if you donated."

My wife is a lovely person and always has other people in mind.

I was so happy and said, "Honestly, I've been thinking about it for a while."

A looming deadline

What I didn't know at the time was that 45 is the cut-off for donation, which is how old I was when my wife and I discussed it.

So I got onto it straight away.

I contacted a donor program operated by a fertility care provider in Australia.

There were some forms to fill in. You have some blood tests and genetic screening done.

What to consider before donating sperm While donating sperm can be considered a generous act, there is a lot to consider before doing so.

The process also involved a questionnaire for things like books I've read, my favourite movies, any hobbies I have. It asked about jobs and education, a little bit about family.

You also share details like your eye colour, cultural background. This all helps the recipient have a bit more understanding about you.

I provided photos of when I was three and six years old.

The other component was a psychological screening in the form of speaking to a counsellor.

And if you're married, you need to let them know. My wife had a separate conversation with the counsellor.

She really coached us through what a big deal this is; not something to be taken lightly.

You're not a father, you're a donor.

You don't have any legal obligation or attachment to the child you help create.

I would welcome a donor child contacting me

The counsellor also asks about how you would feel if the children were to make contact.

[Donor-conceived individuals can access a donor's identifying information when they reach between 16 to 18 years of age, depending on state legislation.]

I said I would more than welcome it. It would be a wonderful thing to meet any of them.

But I also understand you have to be prepared for no-one to contact you ever. You have to be comfortable with that.

As a donor, you really have to park all personal things like, "I'd love to see what that child looks like."

You can think about it, of course, but you can't expect that curiosity to be satisfied.

September 14 to 20 is World Childless Week. If you have a story about childlessness, we'd be honoured to hear from you

A fulfilling experience

When I first heard a child was born, that was when I actually told my parents.

They were so happy, they weren't even shocked.

Initially, I didn't broadcast it to people.

Now, when it comes up in conversation, like when people ask, "Do you have any kids?", I say no; then as I get to know them better, I might share that I have donated.

It's been good to get people's reactions and let them know parts of the process they might not have been aware of.

On my last check, there were five children born using my sperm.

I would say after accepting being childless, this has given me a bounce in my step.

It's fulfilling to know there are children out there. It's helping people. I feel good about that.

title: Bilby capital of Australia turns mascot into 300kg cement sculptures
text:
One of Australia's most beloved tiny marsupials has gone larger than life, with six sculptures set to take over a town in outback Queensland.

Artists have unveiled six cement bilby sculptures in prominent spots across Charleville to celebrate the marsupial's national day on Sunday.

The "bilby release" highlights the town's title as Australia's bilby capital and aims to educate visitors about the endangered species.

Visitors and locals celebrated the trail's launch on National Bilby Day, including Murweh Shire Mayor Shaun "Zoro" Radnedge (right). (Supplied: Bilby Art Trail Charleville)

Trail brings together art and nature

Charleville Cultural Association Arts project manager Carmel Williams said six artists were selected to paint the 300-kilogram cement casts based on their proposals.

"It just all came together beautifully, and each one is unique, with their different style," she said.

Six artist proposals were accepted to paint the bilbies, with the three unsuccessful applicants encouraged to apply for a future bilby release. (Supplied: Carmel Williams)

Ms Williams adapted the idea for the project after visiting the Kooka! Trail in the Brisbane suburb of Paddington in 2022.

But then began the task of raising money to create a cement mould and finding artists to decorate the bilbies.

An exhibition at the Mulga Lands Gallery features local artists and those who worked on the bilby trail. (Supplied: Carmel Williams)

The cement bilbies are positioned in busy parts of town, including the airport, railway station and courthouse.

Over the coming years, it is hoped the trail will grow to 18 bilbies and include other towns in Murweh shire.

"It gives us an opportunity to shine the light on Save the Bilby Fund and the plight of the bilby," Ms Williams said.

Richard Ranson chose to paint in a bold abstract theme. (Supplied: Bilby Art Trail Charleville)

Abstract and traditional artists decorate bilbies

While most of the artists had to travel to Charleville to paint their bilbies, Richard Ranson had the luxury of taking his time and waiting for the right conditions to paint.

Now he walks past his bilby every day, displayed in Graham Andrews Parklands.

The bilby trail takes visitors through prominent and scenic places in Charleville. (Supplied: Richard Ranson)

"We've tried to place them so that when they take the photo, they've got a nice backdrop," Mr Ranson said.

"They're a great design. You can't look at them and not smile."

He said it showed what the town could do.

"It really does bring together the community, and it brings together the arts and the children. Children love them."

Louise Dean (left) travelled to Charleville to paint her bilby in four days. (Supplied: Bilby Art Trail Charleville)

Bilbies released into Qld National Park With the population booming inside a predator-proof fence, conservationists have set the bilbies free. But can they survive on the outside?

Pentland artist Louise Dean was inspired by the Charleville Cosmos Centre, the Moreton Bay Ash gum tree and the town's red dirt.

But she said she felt the pressure as she worked to finish her artwork during a brief visit to Charleville, about 800 kilometres from her hometown.

"Presenting a two-dimensional picture to an art exhibition like that is different to actually going and painting three-dimensional," she said.

Louise Dean practised her design on a paper mache and wire model built by her husband. (Supplied: Louise Dean)

"I have to admit it was a challenge. It was damned hard work, but it all came together in the end, and then they were very thrilled with it.

"It's the most fantastic feeling to have your artwork on display like that and to have a town think that your artwork is worthy enough to put on display."

title: Worker hit by vehicle after pipe blast in underground mine
text:
Queensland's mining regulator has issued a safety alert after a man was critically injured at a central Queensland mine.

A 71-year-old male worker was treated for significant chest, facial, arm and abdominal injuries after emergency services were called to the Crinum underground mine around 10am on Saturday.

He was taken to Emerald and Rockhampton hospitals before being flown to the Royal Brisbane and Women's Hospital on Monday morning, where he remains in a critical condition.

The Gregory Crinum complex is made up of the Gregory open-cut operations and Crinum underground mine. (ABC Capricornia: Vanessa Jarrett)

The mine is part of the Gregory Crinum Complex, which contains an open cut and underground mine, located 60 kilometres north-east of Emerald in the Central Highlands and owned and operated by company Sojitz Blue,

Initial investigations by Resources Safety and Health Queensland (RSHQ) found the worker was carrying out maintenance work on a pipe system when he was hit by a mine vehicle.

RSHQ's report stated the man was standing on the front bumper of a mine vehicle, known as a drift runner, to access the pipework and as he tightened the clamp, the pipe blew, causing pressurised air to blast, creating dust and reducing visibility, and the man fell.

It is then understood the operator of the drift runner, for unknown reasons, moved the vehicle, which struck the man on the ground, the regulator's report said.

In the publication of its safety alert, RSHQ said before starting work on pressurised systems, coal mine operators should ensure workers isolate and depressurise systems, not stand in an area where an unplanned release of energy could occur and establish an exclusion zone.

The safety alert also stated work should be undertaken using suitable work platforms, and not use mobile equipment for that purpose.

RSHQ is continuing investigations into the incident, has isolated the scene and "suspended certain operations until they can be performed to an acceptable level of risk".

The Mining and Energy Union's (MEU) industry safety and health representatives are also involved in the investigations.

"Our thoughts are first and foremost with the injured worker, his family, first responders and his workmates following this serious incident," an MEU statement said.

"We will continue to support our members and the broader workforce as the full circumstances of the incident are established."

title: HYROX apologises after Aussie athlete soils herself mid-race
text:
A founder of HYROX has apologised after an athlete who suffered sudden faecal incontinence mid-competition was allowed to continue, with the incident sparking rule changes after backlash online.

Australian athlete Joanna Wietrzyk experienced the medical episode during the competition that she went on to win in Beijing at the weekend.

The incident went viral on Chinese social media, with videos of her competing while visibly soiled shared widely.

HYROX sees competitors combine running with multiple workout station challenges, including sandbag lunges, burpees, sled pushes and rowing using shared equipment.

Joanna Wietrzyk (middle in black top) holds the HYROX Women's Solo Pro world record. (Instagram: joannawietrzyk)

Following the incident, many online criticised HYROX's health and safety standards, while some also questioned athlete responsibility.

"Blast HYROX. Blast the race director," Chris Hersh posted on a HYROX community Facebook page.

"But please leave the athlete alone or have a tiny bit of empathy for someone that really just was in a horrible situation and got zero assistance from anyone in a high pressure, make a decision on the fly scenario."

HYROX co-founder Moritz Fürste took to Instagram to apologise "to all who were directly or indirectly involved".

"HYROX made a mistake by not reacting immediately during the race," Fürste said in a statement on Instagram.

"In the end it is my job to foresee these potential incidents — and I did not."

He said that new event procedures and rules were being drawn up to "prevent situations like this from happening again".

The rules now state that if a "racer's blood, vomit, urine, or faeces poses a welfare or contamination risk to the racer or to other racers, a Race Director may withdraw the racer from the race on medical grounds".

Before the rule change, competitors were penalised for littering, spitting, or clearing their nostrils onto the race course, which some online described as a double standard.

Following the event in Beijing, HYROX World issued a statement saying that "protocols designed for elite competition and mass participation became blurred, creating ambiguity in how they were applied and understood".

HYROX China said the competition area was cleaned after the competition finished and relevant equipment was removed.

It also said it would replace the floor at the venue to protect future athletes.

The incident went viral in China, with many taking aim at HYROX organisers and rules. (Weibo, RedNote and Douyin)

Wietrzyk, an elite HYROX athlete, was invited to compete at the Beijing event.

She has been contacted for comment.

The ABC has also contacted HYROX for comment.

HYROX is held in indoor venues, with a consistent race format that lets athletes compete against each other worldwide.

Organisers say it suits both elite athletes and people trying to improve their general fitness.

title: Young Brisbane Lions star Logan Morris re-signs with reigning premiers
text:
Young Brisbane Lions star Logan Morris has signed a two-year contract extension, tying him to the club until the end of 2029.

The 21-year-old, who earned his first All-Australian blazer this year, was set to be one of the biggest names on the market at the end of next season.

The signing comes as the Lions prepare to take on the Hawks in a preliminary final on Saturday at the MCG.

"There’s no point dragging [contract negotiations] out if I know what I want to do, and I wanted to stay at Brisbane," Morris said.

"I wanted to just get it done and now I can focus on this week, and hopefully the next few years will be exciting."

Morris kicked 67 goals in the 2026 home-and-away season, finishing second in the Coleman Medal behind Sydney's Charlie Curnow.

It marks the third huge signing coup for the Lions in a week, after Zac Bailey and Dayne Zorko also extended their careers with the club.

When asked about interest from other clubs that may have made higher offers, Morris said he had not given much thought to the money.

"I just thought … more about what I'm happy with and the team that I'm at; I don't want to leave a team where I'm happy where I am mentally and I've got a good group of mates," he said.

"I think playing within a good team that’s got good values and playing with all my mates is more valuable to me than a bit more money, so that's what it ultimately came down to."

text:
A prominent athlete has told court he sent Alan Jones messages wishing him the best for the holidays even after he was allegedly kissed without consent, because the veteran broadcaster had been "generous" to him throughout his life.

The man, known only as Complainant M, has alleged Mr Jones kissed him on the side of the mouth without consent at a public event in 2015.

Complainant taken through timeline of text messages The prosecution has asked why Complainant M called and texted Mr Jones to wish him Merry Christmas and a Happy New Year in 2020. On Tuesday, Crown Prosecutor Georgina Wright SC asked the complainant why he would wish Mr Jones "the best" after being allegedly sexually touched by him several months prior.

"I was being polite I made reference yesterday to the challenges of the relation between myself and the defendant," the complainant said.

"Someone [Mr Jones] that has presence in the media, someone that has a reputation around what they do.

"Someone also who has been generous to me at times in my life, that's why I believe I'm wishing them the best for Christmas even though an incident has occurred prior to this at their house."

Under cross-examination by defence barrister Gabrielle Bashir SC, the complainant was asked about Mr Jones often calling him a "champion", and previously told the athlete "If someone hasn't told you, let me be the first person to tell you, you're special".

"You were an extraordinary athlete, weren't you?" Ms Bashir asked. "Thank you," the complainant replied. "You were something special, weren't you?" Ms Bashir suggested. "I believe I still am," the complainant said.

The complainant agreed with Ms Bashir that Mr Jones had assisted him during times of personal crisis including when he was facing financial difficulties.

title: Lack of volunteers sees Pride events cancelled in regional WA
text:
Organisers of queer festivals in regional Western Australia say their events are at risk of vanishing due to a lack of people willing to help coordinate every year, as another Pride parade bites the dust.

In Carnarvon, about 900 kilometres north of Perth, those pressures have brought the town's 2026 parade to an end after three years, despite being well supported in the community.

Most of the committee behind Queernarvon has stepped down or moved away, leaving the group without enough volunteers.

More than 300 people attended the first year of Queernarvon events. (Supplied: Sophia Alston)

In the state's south, Busselton's long-running Pride parade has also been cancelled, with organisers instead directing their limited resources towards education and wellbeing events.

But in the Pilbara, a Pride festival that began as a small games night among friends has grown to attract about 1,500 people, with organisers crediting support from the wider community for its success.

So, what are the obstacles for LGTBIQA+ people living in the regions?

Changing views

Queernarvon chair Carmen Reilly said Pride events played an important role in regional communities.

In her view, there had been a shift in public perception towards trans, gender diverse and young LGBTQI+ people.

Carmen Reilly (right) says pride events help to connect people. (Supplied: Andrew Robertson)

"I have had several conversations over the last few months with people who have never met a trans person, but have seen posts and AI clips on social media and have formed their opinions," she said.

"I say to those people, 'If you're basing your opinions and ideas on social media, put the phone down, go out and meet someone who has a different life experience to you.'"

She said events such as these helped build real connections within communities.

"There's more connecting us than dividing us," she said.

Finding a community

Johnathan Trace, who is working in Carnarvon on a holiday visa, said he made the decision to leave his home country of the United States because the rise of the far right made him feel unsafe as a trans man.

"I was like, 'It's time. I need to get out of here,'" he said.

Johnathan Trace says people like him are having to carry a huge mental load with the rise of the far right around the world. (ABC Pilbara: Rachel Hagan)

Since being in Australia, Mr Trace said he had felt safer but still experienced moments that made him feel unsafe and unwelcome.

Those ranged from nasty comments delivered by strangers in the bathroom, to homophobic outbursts from customers he was serving at work.

Mr Trace said it was a shame the Carnarvon event was cancelled, as there were a lack of spaces to discuss his life experiences as a trans man.

"You're surrounded by all these backpackers who are just here for a good time, who don't want to talk about politics or anything that ruins their good vibes," Mr Trace said.

" It's very hard to find a real community where you can talk about your queerness and the negative things you face with that. "

Johnathan Trace has travelled across the world to find a community that accepts him living as himself. (ABC Pilbara: Rachel Hagan)

Mining towns lead the way

A bright spot for WA Pride celebrations is in the state's mining region.

The Pilbara Pride Festival started from a small games night among friends, but is now in its fifth year, with about 1,500 people estimated to attend the events across places such as Port Hedland, Karratha and Onslow.

PHLAGS+ runs events across the region for the Pilbara Pride Festival. (Supplied)

Port Hedland Lesbian, Allies, Gays Society (PHLAGS+) secretary Gloria Jacob put the success down to dedicated volunteers and support from local government and the resources sector.

"This year in particular, the one thing that filled my cup was the high school students asking us to hold a workshop at the school, and the high school allowing us to do that," Ms Jacob said.

But she said it had not always been this way.

"I can tell you there were times in the early days where it wasn't that pleasant, and it still isn't pleasant," she said.

" But the main reason we do it is to ensure our young people, our First Nations people and those who are less able to access these safe spaces know PHLAGS+ exist. "

'Space to be themselves'

A local church initially protested against the PHLAGS+ Pride events.

"But the second year they actually marched with us in the parade," Ms Jacob said.

"The more people engage and the more people become aware — it becomes the norm."

Pride events in regional areas attracted visitors from across the state. (Supplied: Sophia Alston)

Ms Jacob said if support was not upheld by the wider community, the regions will lose their diversity.

"If they don't feel like they are welcome or supported or have space to be themselves openly, you're going to lose them to the city," she said.

"The city can be brought to the communities, we've proven it through Pilbara Pride."

title: Second strike planned by Arts Centre Melbourne employees
text:
Advertisement

Workers at Arts Centre Melbourne plan to walk off the job for a second time within a week as part of an industrial dispute over pay. The strike on Friday will likely impact shows across the Arts Centre complex, including one-night-only concert Eclipse: Pink Floyd Orchestrated, performances by circus act Zerial and dance work Burn the Floor: Luminous. The State Theatre at the Arts Centre has been closed for a three-year renovation. Mark Gambino New exhibition Encore! at the Australian Museum of Performing Arts will likely also be affected. Set to open on Wednesday, the exhibition draws on the Arts Centre’s own collection, and includes items such as Kylie Minogue’s gold hot pants from the film clip to her song Spinning Around and the late Midnight Oil drummer Rob Hirst’s drum kit. An Arts Centre Melbourne spokesperson confirmed on Tuesday afternoon that management had been notified of a second strike planned by staff for Friday.

Advertisement

Last week’s strike led to the cancellation of a concert at Hamer Hall by Grammy-winning singer Macy Gray, as well as scheduled performances of GRIMM and dance work Burn the Floor: Luminous in the Arts Centre building. While Gray’s concert has been rescheduled to October 13 and GRIMM’s season has concluded, Burn the Floor has been caught up in the cancellations for a second time. The second strike comes on the back of a long-running pay dispute, as this masthead reported on September 9 (see below): Macy Gray concert at Arts Centre cancelled as staff prepare to strike A concert by Grammy-winning singer Macy Gray at Hamer Hall has been cancelled due to a proposed 24-hour strike by workers at Arts Centre Melbourne. Friday night’s scheduled performances of theatre show GRIMM and dance work Burn the Floor: Luminous in the Arts Centre’s theatres building have also been cancelled ahead of the planned industrial action.

Advertisement

Hamer Hall will be closed all day on Friday and the Arts Centre Melbourne car park “scaled back” for “safety reasons” as a result of the industrial action from 12.01am on Friday, which will include a picket line in the afternoon and public rally in the evening. An Arts Centre spokesperson said ticket holders were being notified about the disruption to shows and that a new date would be announced for Gray’s performance. The Grammy Award-winning American singer Macy Gray, whose Melbourne concert has been cancelled due to industrial action. AP “We will contact ticket holders directly, and thank them for their patience. “Once confirmed, a new date will be announced and all ticket holders to the cancelled performance will be contacted directly.”

Advertisement

A representative for Macy Gray told this masthead the singer would not be commenting on the cancellation of her Melbourne concert, one of a number of dates around Australia on her current tour. Arts Centre Melbourne, Australia’s largest performing arts complex, is owned by the state government and is managed by a trust whose members are appointed by Victoria’s governor at the recommendation of the creative industries minister. Arts Centre Melbourne and its famous spire lit up at night. Leigh Henningham Staff who are members of the Community and Public Sector Union and the Media Entertainment Arts Alliance are taking protected industrial action as part of a long-running dispute over pay. The unions say that nearly 40 per cent of the Arts Centre workforce is on the lowest pay band – band 1 – many of whom are paid the minimum award wage.

Advertisement

Related Article Arts Strike by Arts Centre workers threatens to disrupt Macy Gray concert Employees were offered a 3 per cent increase this year, limited due to a wage cap imposed by the state government. The unions said the offer did not keep up with inflation and was effectively a pay cut. Asked if the negotiations with the union would restart this week, the Arts Centre spokesperson said: “We respect the right of workers to take protected industrial action, and we’re working closely with our team and their unions to progress a new agreement.” Union members are asking for back pay to October 2025, when the previous enterprise agreement expired, protections against artificial intelligence, standardised shift penalties and five days sick leave for casuals (who represent two-thirds of the centre’s workforce). This is the first time in decades that Arts Centre workers have gone on a 24-hour strike. CPSU Victorian branch secretary Jiselle Hanna said the decision to interrupt Macy Gray’s show was not made lightly, “but we are left with no choice until the government funds the Arts Centre properly”.

Advertisement

Hanna said the Victorian government had slashed arts funding in recent years, and called on Creative Industries Minister Vicki Ward to increase its allocation to the Arts Centre. “Vicki Ward has the opportunity to sweep in and stop this industrial action by committing to paying workers fairly,” Hanna said.



“Arts Centre workers need a pay offer that keeps pace with inflation, so they can continue to provide entertainment and high-quality experiences to millions of visitors each year.



“When world-class arts institutions aren’t [sufficiently] funded it’s not just the workers who are impacted, it’s the performers, singers, actors, and the community who benefit so greatly from our arts sector.” Arts Centre Melbourne’s venues include the 884-seat Playhouse. title: Goodbye The Bear and hello Widow’s Bay, as the Emmys crown a new comedy champion
text:
Advertisement

CultureTV & radioEmmys Goodbye The Bear and hello Widow’s Bay, as the Emmys crown a new comedy champion Michael Idato September 15, 2026 — 2:03pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The comedy horror series Widow’s Bay, medical drama The Pitt, the reality competition series The Traitors and the evergreen award-season favourite Hacks swept the 78th annual Emmy Awards. In a not-quite-a-changing-of-the-guard, the sweep signalled that the television conversation has moved on swiftly – perhaps a sign of the times – from The Bear, Beef and Stranger Things. Matthew Rhys poses in the press room with the awards for outstanding lead actor in a limited or anthology series or movie for The Beast In Me, and outstanding lead actor in a comedy series for Widow’s Bay. AP Photo/Richard Shotwell The night’s first and most deserving standing ovation went to Jean Smart, who won lead actress in a comedy. Smart has had a decorated dream run on the series, winning the category four times since 2021. (Abbott Elementary’s Quinta Brunson won in 2023.) Matthew Rhys won best actor twice – lead actor in a comedy (Widow’s Bay) and limited series (The Beast Within Me). Another unsurprising, deserving winner: actor Noah Wyle, lead actor in a drama (The Pitt), with Wyle describing fellow nominee Gary Oldman as “the benchmark I want to hit in my career”.

Advertisement

Related Article Live

Emmys Emmys 2026 as it happened: Widow’s Bay wins sixth award; The Pitt wins outstanding drama series The highlights? John Mulaney, introducing lead actor in a drama. “Since the creation of television, men have been historically unrepresented,” he quipped. And former Game of Thrones star Emilia Clarke, introducing the actress in a limited series segment in her mother tongue, High Valyrian. (Sally Field won, beating Australian actress Sarah Snook in the same category; it was Fields’ fourth win ever, for Remarkably Bright Creatures.) And a surprise cameo from Taylor Swift, playing a rookie detective in a pre-taped skit challenging the Law and Order: SVU cast to answer the biggest mystery of the night: would Swift herself show up at the Emmys? (She did not; she was 2000 kilometres away at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, Missouri, watching her husband Travis Kelce play in the Kansas City Chiefs v Denver Broncos match.) Mariska Hargitay and Taylor Swift with her cat Olivia Benson in the Law and Order Emmys skit. Screenshot So, who was not on the stage? The Bear was nominated for comedy series and Ayo Edebiri for lead actress in a comedy, but the show’s star Jeremy Allen White didn’t crack the lead actor category this year. It feels like an omission; he won in 2023 and 2024.

Advertisement

Netflix’s Stranger Things was similarly shut out. The super-buzzy streaming drama did get a swag of nominations, winning only one (for visual effects) at the Creative Arts Emmys earlier this month, but the series’ fifth and final season was shut out of the acting and directing categories. Loading The “in memoriam” segment opened with an acknowledgment of the passing of Schitt’s Creek star Catherine O’Hara. “She may have forgotten me – twice – but we will never forget her,” actor Macaulay Culkin quipped. (O’Hara played his mother in the Home Alone franchise.) Other notable figures featured in the “in memoriam” included Kiwi actor Sam Neill, costume designer Bob Mackie, director James Burrows, CNN founder Ted Turner, Grey’s Anatomy and Euphoria star Eric Dane, Nashville star Hayden Panettiere, actor James Van Der Beek and beloved actor-director Rob Reiner. Breaking down in tears on stage, actress Jamie Lee Curtis described Reiner as “generous and kind to all”. The package was accompanied by Grammy-nominated artist Noah Kahan performing Bridge Over Troubled Water.

Advertisement

Related Article Emmys Records broken and rallying cries for real television: Full list of winners at the 2026 Emmy Awards The tribute to country singing legend – and film and television star – Dolly Parton was led jointly by singer (and sitcom star) Reba McEntire and actress Sally Field. “If there are truly angels on earth, then we have just lost one,” Field said. McEntire sang one of Parton’s compositions, Appalachian Memories. In addition to the tears, the telecast came with a double shot of a much kinder emotion – nostalgia. Sarah Michelle Gellar and David Boreanaz – who played Buffy and Angel in Buffy: The Vampire Slayer, also appeared on the Emmy stage, to mark the 30th anniversary of the series. Jean Smart poses in the press room with the award for outstanding lead actress in a comedy series for Hacks. AP And three of the stars of Charlie’s Angels – actresses Kate Jackson, Jaclyn Smith and Cheryl Ladd – made an appearance to mark the show’s 50th anniversary which ignited another unsurprising, deserving standing ovation, even if it still does not fully capture the very tangible sentiment in the room for those three iconic women.

Advertisement

The show’s host, actor Mariska Hargitay, acknowledged the 78th year of the awards, and the 100th year of NBC, the network broadcasting them in the US. She was a safe choice as host – widely liked, and connected to a meaningful Hollywood legacy: her mother was the screen icon Jayne Mansfield. And, “Amy [Poehler] and Tina [Fey] said no,” Hargitay quipped. Loading Between the Creative Arts Emmys, held earlier this month in LA, and the Primetime Emmys, 121 Emmys are given out. (That’s before we get to the news, engineering and daytime Emmys.) The Bob Hope Humanitarian Emmy was given to actor Michael J. Fox, in recognition of “his transformative contributions to Parkinson’s disease research and advocacy”. It is only the sixth time the award has been bestowed since its creation in 2002. Despite a robust presence in the nominations, Australia walked away with just four Emmys, all won at the Creative Arts ceremony. Among the nominees: animator Michael Cusack for his animated Smiling Friends, commercial director Kim Gehrig for a Levi jeans TV ad, special effects supervisor Marc Varisco for Monarch: Legacy of Monsters, casting director Jane Norris for All Her Fault and more.

Advertisement

Noah Wyle accepts the award for outstanding lead actor in a drama series for The Pitt. AP Photo/Chris Pizzello And the winners? Love on the Spectrum film editor Marcus Kjellberg, producers Karina Holden and Cian O’Clery for the show’s win in outstanding unstructured reality program, and a second statue for O’Clery, who won the Emmy for casting. The loss we felt the deepest? Australian creative director Julio Himede, nominated twice in the production design for a variety special category, for the Apple Music Super Bowl LX Halftime Show Starring Bad Bunny, and for the 68th Annual Grammy Awards. The Halftime Show won for choreography, directing, lighting design, music direction, sound mixing and technical direction. To deny them the production design win felt like an oversight. Allison Janney accepts the award for outstanding supporting actress in a drama series. AP Among the other Creative Arts winners: the Netflix film Remarkably Bright Creatures (for television movie), Tucci in Italy (hosted nonfiction series or special), The Traitors host Alan Cumming (host of a reality or reality competition program), the Amazon series Spider-Noir (main title design, sound mixing, special visual effects, stunt co-ordination) and Rob Reiner (guest actor in a television comedy) for his role in The Bear.

title: Emmys 2026 as it happened: Widow’s Bay wins sixth award; The Pitt wins outstanding drama series
text:
The Widow’s Bay cast (from left) Jeff Hiller, Matthew Rhys, Dale Dickey, Kingston Rumi Southwick, Kevin Carroll, Stephen Root, Kate O’Flynn and Neil Casey. AP

There were 19 awards handed out in this ceremony, excluding the humanitarian award given to Michael J. Fox. And the big winner on the night was Apple TV.

The streamer won six awards for Widow’s Bay, two for Pluribus and one for Slow Horses, giving it nine in all. That put it way ahead of the pack.

Next best was HBO Max, which won five, across four programs (OK, you might argue that indicates a greater breadth, but whatever). Hacks won best comedy actress for Jean Smart – her fifth win in five seasons of the series, a remarkable streak – plus two for The Pitt and one each for DTF St. Louis and Task.

Netflix won three, for The Diplomat and The Beast In Me (helping Matthew Rhys make history as the first man to win two lead actor awards in the same year, the other coming for Widow’s Bay), and the feature Remarkably Bright Creatures, which gave Sally Field another acting trophy for her bulging cabinet (she has three other Emmy wins, two Golden Globes, a SAG award and a lifetime achievement award, and two best actress Oscars).

title: High-grade WA titanium hit puts McLaren on the money

McLaren Minerals has hit a thick, high-grade zone of titanium-bearing sands right from the surface, with a standout drill intercept of 24 metres grading 7.54 per cent heavy minerals (HM) at its namesake project in the Eucla basin, Western Australia. The impressive hit headlined the latest 61-hole batch of assays from the company’s 2026 resource upgrade and expansion drilling program. Notably, across all 61 holes, the length-weighted average came in at a hefty 4.57 per cent HM over a remarkable average thickness of 21.2m, with every single interval starting from surface. McLaren Minerals has hit an impressive 24 metres at 7.54 per cent heavy minerals at its wholly-owned McLaren titanium project in Western Australia. Results from 1293m of drilling showed impressive consistency, with 70 per cent of the holes returning an average grade of at least four per cent HM. A solid one-third of the holes averaged 5 per cent HM or better. The fact that mineralisation begins at surface and shows considerable thickness is significant, pointing to potentially low-cost, free-dig mining with a minimal strip ratio.

Advertisement

‘All of these results exceed the grade of the 2025 mineral resource of 529Mt at 4.5 per cent heavy minerals.’ McLaren Minerals managing director Simon Finnis Other notable results from the program include a 13-metre hit at 7.25 per cent HM from surface and a 27-metre strike grading 5.83 per cent HM, also from surface. Within the broader zones, pockets of even higher-grade material were found, with nine holes returning one-metre assays of at least a hefty 10 per cent HM, peaking at a stellar 20.10 per cent. The latest results continue a trend of solid drilling outcomes for McLaren, with the grades consistently coming in above the project’s existing mineral resource estimate. That inventory already tips the scales at a whopping 529 million tonnes grading 4.5 per cent HM, containing 23.7Mt of in-situ heavy minerals, split between 249Mt in the indicated category and 280Mt in the inferred class. McLaren Minerals managing director Simon Finnis said: “It is very pleasing to see more excellent results from McLaren, including some very high-grade results, and some great intercepts, with two averaging more than 7% HM - again, all from surface. Noting that all of these results exceed the grade of the 2025 Mineral Resource of 529Mt @ 4.5% HM gives confidence for the next Mineral Resource Update due later this year.” The 2026 drilling program, comprising a hefty 663 holes for 11,568 metres, is designed to increase confidence in the existing resource and provide crucial data for future technical studies as the company pushes towards a bankable feasibility study. Adding weight to the project, metal prices appear to have come to the party, with recent US Geological Survey data showing rutile holding firm at around US$1450 (A$2033) per tonne and ilmenite at US$350 (A$491) per tonne, providing a solid commercial backdrop for McLaren’s development plans.

Advertisement

Governments now recognise titanium as a critical mineral essential for aerospace, defence and new energy technologies, making the development of large-scale domestic projects such as McLaren increasingly strategically important. While the McLaren project is the company’s main game, it has also moved to establish a second front in its mineral sands growth strategy. The company recently completed the acquisition of the zircon-rich Barossa project in South Australia, giving it another platform for growth in the Eucla Basin. With drilling at McLaren continuing to deliver the goods and each batch of assays seemingly outdoing the last, all eyes will now turn to the upcoming mineral resource update scheduled for later this year. If McLaren can replicate these shallow, high-grade results across a meaningful portion of the deposit, it could significantly boost the project’s economics as it marches down the well-trodden path towards feasibility studies and development. title: ‘We are all devastated’: Old Xavs apologise after administrative failure costs grand final berth
text:
Advertisement

SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘We are all devastated’: Old Xavs apologise after administrative failure costs grand final berth Marc McGowan Updated September 15, 2026 — 1:20pm ,first published September 14, 2026 — 3:10pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The president of a powerhouse Victorian amateur football club forced to forfeit a grand final spot has taken full responsibility for selecting an ineligible player. Old Xaverians’ under-19 premier men’s team won its preliminary final over St Kevin’s on Saturday, but won’t contest the grand final against Old Brighton after a league investigation. Old Xavs have been booted from the VAFA under-19s premier grand final for fielding an ineligible player. Photo © Ari Hatzis The Victorian Amateur Football Association announced late on Sunday night that the Old Xavs would receive a $100 fine and forfeit their five-point victory over St Kevin’s for breaking finals eligibility rules. St Kevin’s, not Old Xaverians, will compete in this weekend’s grand final. This masthead is not suggesting that Old Xavs intended to break VAFA rules.

Advertisement

VAFA rules state that under-19s footballers cannot have played more than 12 games in the season in question in the Talent League – the AFL’s premier junior feeder competition – to retain finals eligibility. The player in question, who was on Oakleigh Chargers’ list and in Greater Western Sydney’s academy this season, exceeded that tally, but met other eligibility criteria, which required him to play at least five games for Old Xavs, including a minimum of two after June 30. This masthead contacted Old Xaverians president Michael Logan, general manager James Woods and under-19 coach Matthew Handley. In a statement on the club’s website, Logan said no one at Old Xavs intended to “deceive or act dishonestly”.

Advertisement

“We accept full responsibility for this error, as VAFA rules state that clubs are accountable for ensuring players’ final eligibility,” Logan wrote. “When the matter was brought to our attention, the club undertook a thorough review of the facts and circumstances surrounding the situation, including grounds for review. “At the conclusion of that review, we made submissions to the VAFA. Upon their further investigations, the VAFA’s position was that the ineligibility decision stood. We accept that position.” Logan said Old Xaverians had protocols in place to manage player eligibility, but that they had “failed” in this instance, so the club would review and strengthen the process to try to avoid this happening again. “The situation was in no way the fault of the player ruled ineligible,” he said.

Advertisement

“The club accepts responsibility for his being in this situation and I know he has received – and appreciates – the full support of his teammates. The way both he and his family have conducted themselves during this matter is a credit to them. “Equally, to the rest of the playing group and their families, the club apologises unreservedly. “We are all devastated that the season has ended like this. We have been greatly heartened by the care and support they have shown one another during a really difficult time.” St Kevin’s president Patrick Mount told this masthead on Monday it was an “unfortunate situation”, but that people at his club flagged the player’s ineligibility with the league once they noticed he played in the game. “There have been people saying we knew about it and kept it deliberately quiet, but team sheets can be changed until the last minute, and you don’t know if a player is actually going to play until you see them on the field,” Mount said.

Advertisement

“I didn’t know who he was personally, but we had a number of people on our side who flagged it, and every player’s profile on PlayHQ is publicly accessible and clearly showed he played 16 games in the Talent League. “The rule is black and white – you can’t play more than 12 [Talent League] games. “We have great respect for them as a football club, they have very good people in charge, and I don’t think this was anything more than an administrative oversight. I don’t think it was a deliberately sinister ploy to seek an unfair advantage.” In a statement, the VAFA said it had investigated and confirmed that Old Xaverians’ under-19 men’s team fielded an ineligible player against St Kevin’s on Saturday. “In accordance with VAFA rule 50, ‘A club which includes a player who is not eligible in a team by which it is represented in a premiership match shall be fined as prescribed in schedule of fines contained in rule 129 ($100) and shall forfeit all matches in which such player played … each such match shall be awarded to the opposing club...’,” the statement read.

Broken Hill Gold has launched a major geophysics program and is mobilising a second drill rig to its 100 per cent-owned White Dam gold-copper project in South Australia, ramping up the hunt for sulphides to determine whether its high-grade Icebreaker discovery is the tip of a much bigger iceberg. The company has started 48 line-kilometres of induced polarisation (IP) and 670 line-kilometres of high-resolution ground magnetics to pinpoint deeper sulphide targets. The surveys are due to be completed by mid-October, with initial results expected then. Broken Hill Gold’s induced polarisation geophysics survey is underway at its White Dam gold-copper project in South Australia. Icebreaker sits in the central White Dam project area, 80km west of Broken Hill, where historical exploration overwhelmingly chased shallow oxide gold suited to heap leaching. Broken Hill Gold struck paydirt, unearthing primary sulphides during ongoing oxide resource drilling and opening a new front beneath ground barely tested by previous explorers. Initial drilling returned a 20-metre hit at 2.5 grams per tonne (g/t) gold and 0.5 per cent copper from 58m, including 6m at 7.5g/t gold and 1.2 per cent copper from 66m. Later work delivered 46m at 1.1g/t gold and 0.3 per cent copper from 37m. Adding to the intrigue, Icebreaker sits within a magnetic anomaly extending for up to 1km and the company has reported the discovery open in all directions.

Advertisement

‘We anticipate the surveys being instrumental in defining clear, high-priority targets at depth, by mid-October.’ Broken Hill Gold managing director Matthew Boyes Broken Hill Gold sees deeper potential beyond Icebreaker. One particular deep hole beneath the nearby historical Hannaford pit returned 29m at 0.7g/t gold from 315m, adding weight to the company’s view that mineralisation beneath Hannaford and Vertigo remains open along strike and down dip. Broken Hill Gold managing director Matthew Boyes said: “Given the mineralisation styles observed in initial drilling, we anticipate the Induced Polarisation and high-resolution ground magnetic surveys being instrumental in defining clear, high-priority targets at depth, with initial results expected by mid-October.” The next phase takes the hunt deeper. A dedicated diamond rig is mobilising to work alongside the current reverse circulation (RC) oxide program, with drilling planned into the Icebreaker sulphide zone and beneath Vertigo and Hannaford. Diamond core will also retrieve sulphide material from Icebreaker andoxide mineralisation at Vertigo for metallurgical testwork, helping assess how the different ore styles could respond to processing as White Dam chases resource growth and moves towards an open-pit restart.

Advertisement

The two-rig setup forms part of an 18-month exploration push already underway, comprising more than 30,000m of RC and diamond drilling, electrical and magnetic geophysics and geochemistry across White Dam and regional targets including Wadnaminga. The work is expected to define and upgrade the resource. In parallel, September oxide drilling at Vertigo North Extended and Hannaford is expected to feed an updated and upgraded resource estimate in the fourth quarter, followed by open-pit optimisation and mine planning. Its Rolling, Hannaford East and Icebreaker targets are also in the near-mine oxide push to restart mining. Beyond the central mine area, Broken Hill is spreading its geophysical net across more than 50 underexplored historical prospects, where key targets were generally drilled no deeper than 80m. Survey coverage extends from nearby Vertigo and White Dam East to Mary Mine, 12km west of the White Dam mine, Wilkins 12km south and Green & Gold 16km southwest. There is plenty of historical smoke to chase. Mary Mine returned 16m at 0.9g/t gold and 2.2 per cent copper, while Green & Gold yielded 36m at 1g/t gold and 0.3 per cent copper. The company acquired White Dam in late 2025, inheriting an operation that previously produced 180,000 ounces. The project benefits from historical pits, heap-leach infrastructure and a gold extraction plant, which is expected to generate the cash to bankroll a broader exploration push.

The wider geological address adds another layer. White Dam sits in the Curnamona Province, which has already demonstrated its capacity to host large copper-gold deposits. Kalkaroo, 40km north, hosts 1.1 million tonnes of copper and 3.1 million ounces of gold. With geophysical crews mapping the subsurface and a second rig poised to punch deeper holes, Broken Hill Gold has two prizes in its sights: push White Dam’s oxide resources towards an open-pit restart while the surveys and drill bit determine whether Icebreaker has exposed the first glimpse of something much bigger underneath.
