Sarytogan Graphite has significantly extended copper mineralisation at its Ilksan prospect in central Kazakhstan, delivering a massive 318-metre-long intersection from surface to the end of the hole. The result comes from the second of a three-hole diamond drill program and follows a similarly impressive 229-metre hit from the first hole. The company says the new hole has confirmed it’s onto a large, fertile copper porphyry system. Visible malachite and azurite in the core from 20 metres downhole from the second hole drilled at Sarytogan Graphite’s Ilskan prospect in Kazakhstan. The latest intersection came in with a headline figure of 318m grading 0.14 per cent copper and 0.027 grams per tonne gold from surface. Within the broad mineralised envelope, several higher-grade zones stand out, including 18.9m at 0.29 per cent copper from just 5m downhole and a solid 15.2-metre section grading 0.4 per cent copper from 163.4m. The result builds on the success of the program’s first hole, which previously returned a 229-metre intercept at an almost identical grade of 0.14 per cent copper from surface. The company says the consistency between the two holes, drilled 150m apart, points to a large-scale system. The Ilksan prospect forms part of the broader Baynazar copper exploration project,just 25km south-west of Sarytogan’s world-class graphite deposit.

Advertisement

‘The diamond drill core and assays at Ilksan demonstrate the presence of a fertile copper porphyry system.’ Sarytogan Graphite managing director Sean Gregory According to Sarytogan, geological indicators such as elevated copper grades, potassic alteration and the presence of “B-veins”, a type of quartz vein commonly associated with porphyry copper systems, suggest the drilling is getting closer to the core of the porphyry system, where higher grades are typically found. At Ilksan, the B veins contain quartz, biotite, magnetite, potassium feldspar and chalcopyrite. Sarytogan Graphite managing director Sean Gregory said: “The diamond drill core and assays at Ilksan demonstrate the presence of a fertile copper porphyry system. The results of the deeper 3rd hole are eagerly anticipated.” The Ilksan discovery is the culmination of a systematic exploration campaign that began with a review of historical Soviet-era records. That work highlighted two shallow drill holes from the 1970’s that hit copper mineralisation, with grades reportedly increasing with depth. Since pegging the ground in 2024, the company has completed high-resolution magnetics, collected more than 6000 soil samples and conducted trenching, which returned a 270m-long intercept at 0.13 per cent copper. Subsequent shallow drilling then defined a 600m-diameter bedrock anomaly with grades up to 0.5 per cent copper, paving the way for the current deeper diamond drill campaign.

Advertisement

The move into copper appears to be a shrewd diversification play, leveraging the company’s established in-country exploration expertise and its deep knowledge of Kazakh permitting. The project sits in a region known for its mining prowess. Kazakhstan is a highly prospective jurisdiction for copper porphyry mines, with some of the world’s lowest-cost copper operations situated there, benefiting from low power, diesel and skilled labour costs. Elsewhere, just 25km to the northeast, recent testwork on a 24-tonne bulk sample of ore at Sarytogan’s flagship graphite deposit landed some eye-catching results. The test produced 30kg of coated spherical purified graphite (CSPG), delivering a hefty 97.7 per cent yield, eclipsing the typical industry range of 50 to 60 per cent. And perhaps more significantly, the end product reached a whopping 99.99 per cent purity, comfortably surpassing the typical 99.95 per cent lithium-ion battery requirement. The company is now preparing a 5kg sample of CSPG to ship to a leading European prototyping organisation. The material will be used to manufacture and test large format pouch cell batteries, a key step in qualifying the product for European offtake partners. With two long, consistent copper intercepts now in the bag, all eyes will likely be on the assays from the third and deepest hole of the program. That hole was drilled a further 150m north and terminated at 452m depth when the budget was exhausted.

If Sarytogan is right and it is indeed closing in on the high-grade core of this big porphyry system, the results from that deeper hole could make things very interesting very quickly for the Perth-based explorer. title: City of Perth faces yet another inquiry – this one, with teeth
text:
Advertisement

The City of Perth faces yet another inquiry as it battles to overcome “fractured working relationships” and “ongoing governance issues” plaguing the council. Local Government Inspector Tony Brown revealed the commencement of his formal inquiry after addressing councillors and city staff at a behind-closed-doors meeting on Monday evening, where he presented them with the findings of a five-month probe that began with the appointment of former Kwinana mayor Carol Adams as a monitor in January. Local Government Inspector Tony Brown outside the City of Perth’s Council House on Monday evening. Cameron Myles Brown told media the fresh inquiry would take about three months and cost about $120,000, however he was confident it would be a “short and effective way of providing an outcome for the City of Perth community”. The council has been in the headlines constantly this year after Adams was appointed to monitor the local government amid a relationship breakdown between councillors and the city administration.

Advertisement

Brown said Adams’ report was not a public document, however the inquiry report would be, and could include recommendations for the council to implement. “We could recommend to the minister for local government that the council be dismissed, or certain individuals be dismissed,” he said. “So that’s the worst-case scenario, and I do not want to pre-empt what the inquiry will find.” Legislatively, Brown cannot take action on Adams’ monitor’s report, which paved the way for his inquiry. Brown listed breaches of confidentiality, a breakdown of public working relationships, and city officers “inundated with way too many questions and requirements” as issues raised during the monitor’s inquiry.

Advertisement

Altogether, Adams’ report led to 12 actions that Brown made clear he expected the city to undertake. “The City of Perth is the flagship local government of Western Australia, so it needs to be the leader in governance,” he said. Related Article Local government Perth council blocks CEO return as investigation continues “I don’t think it’s there at the moment, so we’re going to work through that, and we want the City of Perth to be able to return to providing good governance for its community.” The local government inspector pushed back on suggestions bureaucracy was hindering meaningful action, noting the previous, well-publicised inquiry into the city ran for more than two years and cost $7 million, while his and Adams’ inquiries should be wrapped up within the space of nine to 12 months.

Advertisement

On Tuesday, Brown told ABC Perth he was not happy about issues in the ongoing relationships between elected members that had played out in the public arena, as well as the regular breaches of confidentiality. He said there had been a lot of complaints against councillors, both from within the city administration and the council itself, which showed the elected members were not working together well. “The working relationship between the council and the administration is the main focus, and you need to be working together,” he said. “And where we see individual elected members not wanting to work for their collective community and not wanting to build relationships, these sort of issues happen.” Opposition Leader Basil Zempilas – who was previously the Perth lord mayor before his elevation to state politics – said he was “genuinely disappointed” about the state of affairs at his old council, which he said had worked hard to act on the lessons from the previous inquiry.

Advertisement

“To see the city be back in a position where its reputation is being questioned is deeply distressing to me because I know how hard myself, the new council, and the administration worked together to change that position,” he said on Tuesday morning. “We worked incredibly hard, harmoniously, and always put the ratepayers of the City of Perth first.” City of Perth chief executive Michelle Reynolds was suspended by the council in May after councillors and city staff received a briefing on Adam’s report from Brown, during which he put the council “on notice” regarding the monitor’s probe. The development prompted an angry response from Local Government Minster Hannah Beazley who in turn raised the spectre of council amalgamations. Last month, a motion to bring Reynolds back from suspension “effective immediately” was voted down, with councillors opting to defer the decision until after the completion of a workplace culture review.

Advertisement

Zempilas said the question of Reynolds’ employment situation “does not appear to be answered”, and warned against a situation where the inquiry “drags on and drags on”. “It is incumbent upon councils to work together in the best interests of the ratepayers, and clearly there has been a breakdown here,” he said. “And I’ve got to say, as the capital city for Western Australia, everyone has a right to feel disappointed about what’s taken place there.” Opposition local government spokeswoman Kirrilee Warr questioned the need for another inquiry, declaring: “This has been going on for far too long.” “Hopefully we can get to the bottom of what’s going on at the City of Perth,” she said.

Advertisement

Warr initially held hope that recent reforms that led to the creation of the local government inspector’s office would make a difference in the sector, but now has her doubts. “I think this Labor government hasn’t been clear with local government around what is the plan,” she said. “They are very good to drop hot minute statements across media or in forums to lead people down a path to think that there will be a result, but right now we are seeing a number of councils being called in once again around their behaviours, around relationships, and around how they’re conducting themselves, and that is not good for anyone.” The City of Perth was the first council to be allocated a monitor, just two weeks into Brown’s role as the head local government watchdog at the start of the year.

US rapper Macklemore says he was dropped as the support act for Ed Sheeran’s American tour after making pro-Palestine comments on stage this month. The Thrift Shop rapper stood by his “Free Palestine” comments, made during a performance at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium this month, in a detailed Instagram post that attracted criticism from a US-based pro-Israel activist group and the singer Pink. The Grammy Award-winning artist, whose real name is Benjamin Haggerty, broke records with his 2013 hit Thrift Shop with Ryan Lewis and featuring Wanz, becoming the second independently distributed song to reach number one on Billboard’s Hot 100. Sheeran has not commented, and a replacement opening act for his tour is yet to be confirmed. How did we get here? The controversy began at MetLife Stadium on September 4, during his support spot for Sheeran, when Macklemore exclaimed “Free Palestine” while introducing his protest song Hind’s Hall, and showed footage of the devastation in Gaza on a screen. Macklemore and Ed Sheeran, pictured in 2014, have been longtime friends. title: Could a Scottish, Welsh and Northern Irish independence pact threaten UK unity?
text:
In brief The Scottish National Party, Wales' Plaid Cymru and the pro-Irish unity Sinn Féin want to break away from the UK.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has previously rejected Northern Ireland or Scotland holding referendums on the matter.

Leaders of the main Scottish, Northern Irish and Welsh nationalist parties declared at a meeting overnight that they have the right to choose whether to stay in the United Kingdom, with all three seeing their future as nations within the European Union.

The Scottish National Party (SNP), Plaid Cymru in Wales, and the pro-Irish-unity Sinn Féin want to break away from the UK, although under different timelines and conditions.

The rare meeting in the Welsh capital came just days after United States President Donald Trump waded in on the issue, saying he would back a united Ireland.

His comments showed "the unity debate is very much alive", Northern Ireland's Michelle O'Neill said alongside fellow party leaders as they announced a memorandum of understanding.

"Our nations have the right to self-determination. No Westminster government (the UK government) has the right to block democracy or undermine the principle that our people will decide their own future," the agreement said.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

SNP leader John Swinney, Rhun ap Iorwerth, leader of Plaid Cymru in Wales, and Mary Lou McDonald and O'Neill, leader and deputy leader of Sinn Féin, met in their roles as party leaders, rather than as top officials in their respective governments.

O'Neill is Northern Ireland's first minister while Iorwerth and Swinney lead their respective nationalist parties in Scotland and Wales.

Where do Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland stand on the independence issue?

The agreement said that, for the first time, each nation had a first minister "committed to independence from the UK", adding: "The future of our nations belongs in the European Union."

The independence parties are the biggest in both the Scottish and Welsh parliaments for the first time since devolution measures began in 1999. Sinn Féin has been the biggest party in Northern Ireland's assembly since 2022.

The SNP wants a second independence referendum after an earlier ballot in 2014 saw Scotland narrowly vote to remain in Britain. Successive UK governments have ruled out an immediate rerun.

Sinn Féin, the former political wing of the paramilitary Irish Republican Army (IRA), wants a vote on the UK territory of Northern Ireland being reunified with Ireland.

Plaid Cymru seeks Welsh independence in the longer term, but Iorwerth has ruled out pressing for a referendum immediately.

Could an independence move succeed?

Laura McAllister, a politics professor at Cardiff University, said the deliberately broad term "self-determination" was used due to these differing timelines and goals.

"Plaid Cymru was elected with heavy emphasis on avoiding the issue of independence this term," she told Agence France-Presse (AFP).

Shortly after taking power, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said a referendum on Irish unity was "off the table".

The 1998 Good Friday peace agreement that largely ended three decades of conflict in Northern Ireland provides for a referendum if Westminster's Northern Ireland minister believes a majority is likely to favour joining the Republic of Ireland.

Sinn Féin leader McDonald said the prime minister had no authority to deny any provisions of the agreement, and Burnham backtracked in parliament last week.

On Monday, a spokesperson insisted that Burnham believed "strongly in the Union", the constitutional tie that makes Northern Ireland part of the UK.

On Scotland, Burnham told lawmakers there could be another vote if there was a "clear consensus" but later reportedly said a referendum remained "off limits".

"It is unlikely that this (meeting) will change the UK Government's refusal to allow a referendum in Scotland or, at present, Northern Ireland," said Michael Keating, an emeritus politics professor at the University of Aberdeen.

But the meeting was "significant politically", he told AFP, because the other parties long avoided association with Sinn Féin due to its link to the IRA.

Alex Kane, a former communications chief for Ireland's Ulster Unionist Party, pointed to the absence of Northern Ireland's deputy first minister, Emma Little-Pengelly, of the pro-UK Democratic Unionist Party.

Her post is of equal weight to O'Neill's under Belfast's power-sharing government and "neither can claim to represent the government of Northern Ireland if the other hasn't agreed to it," he told AFP.

Little-Pengelly slammed O'Neill, claiming her position was "weaponised" at "a summit of separatists".

The meeting sparked mixed reactions in Belfast.

"Ireland would be better off if it was one country and we were back in the EU," retiree Ray Dennison, 61, told AFP.

But Jim Boyle, a 64-year-old environmental worker, said the meeting filled him with "trepidation".

"Many years ago I may have wished for the break-up of the United Kingdom, now ... I just don't want anything that's unpredictable."

title: 'Enormously confronting': The uncomfortable truth behind the HYROX defecation controversy
text:
In brief An Australian athlete was pictured with faeces on her legs during a HYROX race in China.

The incident has drawn heated debate about the rules of the competition.

It was an incident that triggered international headlines. But while a HYROX athlete's mid-race bowel movement has raised questions about hygiene and fairness, the urge to go is a familiar reality for many endurance athletes.

HYROX is a fitness and endurance race that combines 8km of running with exercises such as rowing, sled pushes and wall balls, carried out in indoor exhibition halls.

The co-founder of the global sport, Moritz Fürste, apologised on Monday after Australian athlete Joanna Wietrzyk soiled herself during a race in Beijing over the weekend and went on to win.

Footage posted on social media showed Wietrzyk, who holds the sport's women's solo pro world record, competing at stations with faeces on her legs.

"I apologise to all that were directly or indirectly affected, as well as to everyone who felt like we did not handle the situation like we should have," Fürste's statement said.

"HYROX made a mistake by not reacting immediately during the race."

Fürste said the organisation had immediately begun improving its event processes and had introduced new rules and procedures to prevent a similar situation from occurring again.

The incident triggered significant backlash online, with some arguing it had affected other racers' ability to compete in a safe and hygienic environment.

Joanna Wietrzyk is the world record holder in the HYROX women's solo event. Source: Getty / VCG

"These competitors pay hundreds of dollars to participate and spend weeks, if not months, training for these events. Their health, safety, and ability to perform should matter just as much as anyone else's," read one comment which received thousands of likes.

Critics also questioned why officials did not intervene, given HYROX imposes penalties for other acts such as spitting and nostril clearing.

Gut issues and endurance sports

It's not unusual for endurance athletes to experience gastrointestinal symptoms during competition, nor is it unheard of for them to continue despite soiling themselves.

During the 2005 London Marathon, eventual winner Paula Radcliffe stopped and relieved herself in view of TV cameras.

She later explained she had been running through stomach cramps — likely affecting her speed — because of her reluctance to relieve herself in front of "however many thousands of people were watching on television".

READ MORE The secret to good gut health? It starts with eating the rainbow

French race walker Yohann Diniz experienced intestinal issues during the 2016 Olympics, but continued walking for many kilometres despite soiling himself.

According to research by Monash University, strenuous exercise lasting two hours or more — particularly running — appears to exacerbate gut disturbances.

Researchers estimate 30 to 70 per cent of athletes experience gastrointestinal symptoms, with endurance athletes particularly susceptible.

Bec Hoschke, a former professional triathlete and Ironman champion who now coaches endurance athletes in Sydney, told SBS News gut health can be a "highly sensitive thing for many endurance athletes".

The HYROX Beijing event was held over the weekend. Source: Getty / Fred Lee

She said the HYROX incident was a "very difficult situation" for the parties involved: the competition, the athlete and her competitors.

"Athletes make enormous sacrifices for international competition," she said. "For some athletes, it's their living."

She said the issue was not only one of public health and hygiene but also of the health and well-being of the athlete involved.

"I can't imagine the mental impact all of this is having on someone. I think she's only in her early 20s as well. It's enormously confronting for someone to have to deal with at that age."

Wietrzyk reportedly posted on her Instagram story after the race showing herself attached to an IV, writing "go hard or go home they say ... a win is a win", but later deleted the post.

Her coach, Chris Bayens, said what had happened was "extraordinary", "unforeseen" and difficult to comprehend in real time.

"Decisions were made under competition conditions by an athlete, judges and officials, all responding to a situation none of them could reasonably have prepared for," he wrote in an Instagram post.

He said discussion and review of those decisions was legitimate, but "the hatred and personal attacks that have followed are not".

"Sport occasionally produces moments that are imperfect and deeply human."

Hoschke said HYROX presents different considerations to more individualised endurance events like marathon running because athletes compete in a contained space and use shared equipment.

"I hope that the public and the people that are involved in the sport can get something out of this conversation for the benefit of the sport," she said.

title: Millions of Australians set to face spring wintry blast this week
text:

title: 'New low': Zali Steggall weighs in on controversial Sydney Sweeney ad
text:
IN BRIEF US actress Sydney Sweeney is facing criticism from Australian athletes over a new ad.

Independent MP and former Olympian Zali Steggall has criticised a new sexualised sports betting advertisement featuring United States actress Sydney Sweeney as a "new low", amid mounting uproar over its depiction of women in sport.

In her latest controversial ad, Sweeney features naked in the ad for a sports betting company — in some scenes her private parts covered only by footballs or other sports gear.

"They wanted to show just sports," she says while sitting topless on a basketball hoop, before repeatedly saying "sports" in other suggestive poses.

The ad has sparked backlash from current and former female athletes around the world, outraged by its portrayal of women in sport. Some, including Australian water poloist Matilda Kearns, have taken to social media to show "real" women in sport.

Kearns posted a video of her competing in the pool and training at the gym with the caption: "Here's some real women sports content."

"I can't describe how infuriated I feel when I watch this," she said in a since-expired social media post.

"How do we live in a world where monetising a woman's body and sexualising women's sport is still a thing? To take the mickey like this, I thought we were genuinely moving past this bullsh-t."

Steggall, Australia's most successful alpine skier, described the gambling ad as "incredibly disappointing and just offensive".

"It uses a woman's body to sell sports betting while reducing women's sport to a sexualised punchline. It's a trope that we need to do away with and it comes from an industry already targeting young men through sports to gamble to ruin their lives," Steggall said.

She said as a young athlete she was often pressured to do sexualised campaigns showing her body in ways that made her uncomfortable, and "really cheapened me as an athlete".

Zali Steggall is Australia's most successful alpine skier, having performed in four Winter Olympics between 1992 and 2002. Source: AP / David Phillip

"Female athletes have fought for decades to be recognised for what we are, serious competitive athletes — strong and powerful," the MP for the Sydney seat of Warringah said in a social media post.

Steggall appealed to young girls, saying her Olympian's body is strong and powerful and she was proud of what her body was capable of.

"It doesn't look like what Sydney Sweeney and others show. It comes in all shapes and sizes.

"To young men — don't be fooled, this is a gambling company trying to lure you using sex to get your attention so they can lose their money."

It's not the first time Sweeney has courted controversy for an ad. Last year, she was accused of promoting white supremacy after featuring in a campaign for denim brand US Eagle, which featured the tagline, "Sydney Sweeney has great jeans". In the ad, she discussed biological traits passed down from parents.

Drieberg said it perpetuates an unacceptable view that this is how women's bodies should be portrayed and used, and it "adds years" to the fight for gender equality.

"It's been incredible to watch the evolution of women in sports and the respect that athletes have and deserve increase year on and year out.

"When we see campaigns like this ... it puts us back."

title: 'Hoax': Donald Trump dismisses warnings that AI could destroy humanity
text:
In brief Tech leaders have urged regulations requiring independent audits of advanced frontier AI models.

Trump, in a post on social media, said the industry's call for regulation is a "hoax".

United States President Donald Trump has dismissed fears that artificial intelligence could wipe out humanity, calling them a hoax and rejecting global calls to put guardrails around the fast-moving technology.

Trump's pushback comes amid growing international alarm about AI, with even some tech bosses saying development of computer super-intelligence needs to slow down.

Trump said the US could not afford to lose a technological race with rival China and insisted the only guardrails necessary were a "STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!"

"AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX," Trump said in one of a series of posts on his Truth Social network about the subject.

Trump compared it to what he called "all the other hoaxes", including the investigation into ties between his election campaign and Russia, and his impeachment over Ukraine, both in his first term.

Amodei — whose firm Anthropic makes the hugely successful AI system Claude — was quickly backed by OpenAI boss Sam Altman and by former Trump ally Elon Musk, who also owns xAI.

The latest warnings were sparked after OpenAI developers reported scares in which AI models broke out of what were supposed to be secure testing spaces, reached the internet and coordinated to attack Hugging Face, a site where code is stored.

Global concerns about AI and a possible extinction event have dramatically escalated in recent days.

title: 'A lot of work to be done': Australia's major health win faces its next challenge
text:
IN BRIEF HIV diagnoses have fallen significantly in Australia since 2016.

Experts say more equity in testing, prevention and treatment is needed for some groups.

HIV diagnoses have fallen significantly over the past decade, with Australia on track to achieve preliminary UN targets as part of a world-leading response, but experts say progress remains uneven across communities.

The latest Australian HIV and sexually transmitted infection data show that, overall, HIV diagnoses in Australia have fallen 25 per cent in a decade.

From 2016 to 2025, there was a 28 per cent decline in HIV diagnoses among males, and no change among women, a feature of the data attributed to high rates of testing, treatment and use of pre-exposure prophylaxis medicine, known as PrEP, among men who have sex with men.

Australia is a signatory to the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS), which leads the global effort to end AIDS as a public health threat by 2030.

Currently in Australia, 94 per cent of people living with HIV have been diagnosed, 95 per cent of HIV-positive people are receiving treatment. Of that figure, 98 per cent of treatments have resulted in suppressing HIV to undetectable and virtually untransmittable levels.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

While it is expected Australia will achieve the preliminary UNAIDS targets, where 95 per cent of people living with HIV are diagnosed, 95 per cent of those diagnosed are on treatment, and 95 per cent of those on treatment have HIV that is virally suppressed, analysis from the Kirby Institute at the University of New South Wales has shown that some groups are being left behind.

What does the data show?

The HIV notification rate — a figure that accounts for the change in growing populations — showed that the overall rate of HIV notification per 100,000 people had dropped from approximately 4 in 2016 to just under 3 in 2025.

The notification rate was seven times higher among males than females in Australia.

Overall, Australia had a 28 per cent reduction in HIV diagnoses between 2016 and 2025. Source: SBS News / The Kirby Institute

In 2025, the transmission of the majority of HIV cases was attributed to male-to-male sexual contact, at 64 per cent, while 26 per cent were attributed to heterosexual sexual contact, and a small proportion, 3 per cent, were attributed to injection drug use.

Rates of HIV remain low among people who inject drugs in Australia and among sex workers, which Kirby Institute epidemiologist Dr Skye McGregor said reflected the strong and long-running community response to HIV among priority populations.

The groups falling behind

The most recent period, 2025, saw the highest number of HIV diagnoses in First Nations peoples, with 3.9 notifications per 100,000 — 1.9 times the diagnosis rate for Australian-born non-Indigenous people.

McGregor said this reflected a need to work closely with communities to ensure prevention, treatment and testing responses were appropriate.

Experts said it was important to ensure that messaging around testing, prevention and treatment was accessible, to ensure no groups are left behind as Australia achieves HIV targets. Source: SBS News / The Kirby Institute

More than half of gay and bisexual men diagnosed with HIV were born overseas, and from 2016-2025, while diagnoses among gay and bisexual men born in Australia reduced by 48 per cent, for those born overseas, that figure was only 18 per cent.

Scientia professor at the Kirby Institute, professor Andrew Grulich, said that while there have been significant advancements in self-testing and other outreach activities such as the installation of HIV testing vending machines in universities, equity in care was the next challenge.

"When we look at the data, we find reductions in HIV are not as good outside of the city as they are in the city. We need better access to testing and to PrEP outside of the city centres," he said.

While the number of HIV diagnoses was higher for men than women, diagnoses for men declined over a ten-year period, while that figure for women remained the same. Source: SBS News / The Kirby Institute

President of the National Association of People with HIV, Scott Harlum, said Australia was in a good position to confront these issues head-on.

"In Australia we do this better than anywhere else in the world, that's our track record. We have the best people in the world; we have a government that's committed to it; nothing is lacking.

"But there are disparities in these numbers that are only going to be answered by speaking to these communities, especially for new arrivals to the country."

Late diagnosis of HIV was also an emerging issue: in 2025, one-third of diagnoses were considered "late", which often meant someone had been living with undiagnosed HIV for four years.

McGregor from the Kirby Institute said there was a clear need for a range of testing strategies that are accessible for all populations, including Australian-born and overseas-born populations, adding that HIV tests should be normalised as a regular part of sexual health.

"We're lucky to have self-testing in Australia, but we also need accessible healthcare and clinician education, so when someone goes for a sexual health checkup, it should include HIV and gonorrhoea," she said.

Jessica Michaels, deputy chief financial officer at the Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine, said there was "a lot of work to be done" around stigma and discrimination reduction, especially for healthcare workers, who she said were still discussing prevention and testing with people "based on preconceived ideas of who is at risk".

"We really need to move away from that, and to have all healthcare workers thinking 'could it be HIV?' regardless of who is sitting in front of them."

title: Labor appoints former Liberal leader Sussan Ley to Snowy Hydro board role
text:
In brief Labor has tapped former Liberal Party leader Sussan Ley to join the board of the Snowy Hydro 2.0 project.

Many Snowy workers live in Ley's former electorate of Farrer.

A former coalition leader has been appointed by the Labor government to help steer the nation's most expensive and delayed renewable energy project.

Sussan Ley will sit on the Snowy Hydro board following her resignation from politics earlier this year, Climate Minister Chris Bowen announced on Monday.

The wholly government-owned project includes eight power stations and more than a dozen dams, spanning more than 100 kilometres from Thredbo to Tumut in NSW's south.

Snowy 2.0 is now being built and will store excess power from wind and solar, intended to become the centrepiece of the project.

title: Barnaby Joyce reveals more details on One Nation's plan to cut migration
text:
In brief One Nation has announced a plan to slash Australia's temporary migrant population by 750,000 over three years.

The policy has been criticised by government and Opposition figures as damaging for the economy.

One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce said his party will cut Australia's migrant population "primarily by not issuing new" visas, after his party announced a plan to dramatically slash migration and bring it into "net-negative" for three years on Monday.

The policy would cut Australia's temporary migrant population by 750,000 over three years — a move One Nation says would ease pressure on housing and essential services and return the temporary migrant population to 2017 levels.

It includes cuts to student visas, graduate visas, temporary skilled visas and bridging visa holders, as well as the "departure and removal of illegal migrants".

In an interview with News24, Joyce said not allowing the family of temporary skilled workers to apply to join their partners or parents in Australia will cut down migration by more than 100,000 people.

"We bring up [the example of] nurses thinking, Oh well, that’s 50 per cent, or 30 per cent [of skilled migrants]. No, it’s 1 per cent or less, the nurses, and less than 1 per cent is aged care workers.

"We’re getting numbers down primarily by not issuing new visas."

In 2025 the Australian Nursing and Midwifery Foundation reported internationally qualified nurses (IQNs) make up approximately 20 per cent of the total nursing workforce and in aged care this increases to 35 per cent.

Joyce also said universities are being used as a "backdoor" to migration, adding Australia is "going from a country to a caravan park".

"We're still having students come in. We're looking at a cap of 100,000 a year, but we're just not having this sort of universities used as basically a backdoor to migration into Australia," he said.

READ MORE Why fixing Australia's immigration system is not just about cutting migrants

Following the "three-year reset", where more people would leave Australia than arrive, One Nation says its annual cap of 130,000 on net overseas migration (NOM) would remain in place and be reviewed each year.

Net overseas migration measures the difference between the number of people who arrive in Australia and those who depart, including returning Australians.

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke delayed a National Press Club speech in August in which he was widely expected to announce migration cuts. It is understood the cabinet is still finalising plans.

The government previously set a target of 225,000 for 2027-28.

Party leader Pauline Hanson said her plan was about "restoring control and making sure migration serves Australia".

The proposal expands on One Nation's existing migration policy after the party was forced to clarify its position in recent weeks following confusion sparked by comments from One Nation MP David Farley.

'A real shock to the economy'

Members of both Labor and the Coalition criticised the plan in Monday morning media appearances.

Health Minister Mark Butler said the plan would devastate the health and aged care sectors and smash certain industries like construction.

"Pauline Hanson said a few weeks ago, she didn't care what the impact of her migration policy would be on business, but this is just another level entirely," Butler told reporters on Monday.

Meanwhile, deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume told News24 a negative NOM would be a "real shock to the economy and it would make all Australians poorer".

"My concern here is that these numbers have simply been plucked out of thin air, that there isn't any modelling behind them," she said.

Both major parties have sought to restrict their own migration policies, though they've denied those moves are linked to One Nation's growing popularity.

When borders reopened following COVID-19 pandemic closures, Australia saw a surge in arrivals, with net overseas migration peaking at 556,000 in 2022-23.

NOM fell to 301,000 in 2025-26, according to data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics.

title: Swedish election in dead heat as anti-immigration far right loses ground
text:
In brief Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson has headed a minority coalition backed by the far right Sweden Democrats for four years.

The election results will decide whether Kristersson's push toward a hard-right clampdown on migration continues.

Sweden's leftwing opposition bloc held a razor-thin lead in Sunday's general election with half of the votes counted, with the far right seen losing ground.

With more than 50 per cent of votes counted, four opposition parties led by Social Democratic leader Magdalena Andersson, had a narrow lead with 49.3 per cent against 49.1 per cent for Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson's right-wing alliance, which includes the anti-immigration Sweden Democrats.

In a big surprise, the anti-immigration Sweden Democrats lost support for the first time since it entered parliament in 2010, with 17.7 per cent of the vote, down from 20.5 per cent in 2022.

"Of course it's a bit of a disappointment that we are not the second-biggest party anymore in these polls. But it's still not finished, it can still change," Julia Kronlid, a Sweden Democrat member of parliament, told Agence France-Presse (AFP) just after exit polls had showed the party retreating.

Experts predicted the race could go down to the wire.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

In the event of a left-wing victory, the four parties would face tough negotiations to form a government as they are splintered ideologically.

"I am confident that Magdalena is a skilled negotiator, and that she has a plan to make it work ... It might take a bit of time, but we will get a government led by Magdalena," Emilia Wikstrom Melin, a 40-year-old union analyst, told AFP at the Social Democrats' watch party.

What's at stake for Sweden in this election?

Kristersson has headed a minority coalition backed by the Sweden Democrats for four years, giving the far-right influence over policy in exchange for support in parliament.

Kristersson promised the Sweden Democrats key cabinet posts if the right wing wins.

"It would be really tough for the country to go back to four years of the Social Democrats in power," Sweden Democrat supporter Bjorn Englen told AFP.

Throughout the campaign, opinion polls gave a comfortable lead to the left-wing opposition, but the gap narrowed to a dead heat in the final days.

Much of the campaign focused on healthcare and helping struggling households cope with rising costs.

Andersson, the first woman to head Sweden's government in 2021-22, is a staunch defender of Sweden's famed welfare state.

Her party ruled the Scandinavian country for most of the 20th century and remains Sweden's largest, though early results showed the party heading for its worst result in modern history.

Andersson has pledged to raise taxes on banks and high incomes, cut healthcare queues, and improve declining school results.

"We've had four years of rising unemployment, with a salary that pays for less and less," she said in a televised debate before the vote.

Adding a touch of star power to election day, ABBA's Benny Andersson performed at her party's headquarters in Stockholm, changing the lyrics of their hit song "Mamma Mia" to "Mag-da-le-na!".

Outgoing prime minister Kristersson meanwhile vowed to focus on improving Swedes' everyday lives now that his government's clampdown on organised crime and immigration was starting to show results.

Deadly shootings and bombings by organised crime networks have fallen sharply in recent years, while asylum applications are at a record low.

"We want to use our new and far better preconditions to improve the lives of ordinary people ... to make Sweden great again," Kristersson told AFP before the vote, borrowing US President Donald Trump's trademark slogan.

Over the past two decades, far-right leader Jimmie Akesson has steered the party with neo-Nazi roots into the mainstream.

"Sweden is becoming safer, better, and more Swedish," Akesson told a campaign rally on Saturday, surrounded by blue-and-yellow "Make Sweden Sweden Again" posters.

At a polling station on Sunday, store manager Linda Eriksson, 48, told AFP she hoped for a change of government.

"Hopefully a lot of people will realise that we have to change course ... so that everyone will feel included in society," she said.

title: Trump calls on Zelenskyy to stop striking Russian diesel, says attacks are causing a shortage
text:
In brief Ukraine’s long-range strikes have been targeting Russia’s oil and gas industry for months.

Trump also weighed in on Irish reunification during his trip to Ireland.

US President Donald Trump lashed out overnight at Ukraine for targeting Russian oil refineries, vowed to end tariffs on Irish whiskey and played down the threat from artificial intelligence on a two-day trip to Ireland, which again saw him mix diplomacy and personal business interests.

Trump ended his stay by presenting the Irish Open golf trophy to tournament winner Shane Lowry at his Doonbeg golf resort on Ireland's west coast.

The ever-unpredictable American leader said that Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had to do "one thing" and "stop knocking out diesel fuel" refineries in Russia due to growing shortages.

"Let him go after targets, but not diesel fuel, because he's causing a shortage of diesel," Trump said, insisting the Russia-Ukraine war — not the US-Israel conflict with Iran — was to blame.

Oil prices have soared as attacks in the Middle East have intensified, raising American fuel costs and inflation and fueling speculation that the Federal Reserve will hike interest rates just weeks before the US midterm elections.

Russia downgraded its oil output forecast for this year to a 17-year low and revised its fuel exports outlook for 2026 and 2027 due to the war, according to a government draft forecast.

Whiskey tariff, AI safety and Irish reunification

At the end of his visit to Ireland on Sunday local time, Trump said he would remove a 10 per cent tariff on Irish whiskey, a duty that currently applies to all European Union wine and spirit exports to the United States.

Trump made the announcement in front of a crowd of golf fans at the Irish Open. He met Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin in Dublin on Saturday at the start of a 48-hour visit to the country.

"Taoiseach (Ireland's Prime Minister) and I talked about it and Shane (golfer Shane Lowry) talked about it and everybody has been bugging me saying 'would you do me a favor? It's so unfair what's going on. Could you possibly take the tariffs off of Irish whiskey?" Trump said.

"And I said on behalf of the United States of America, I am going to take the tariffs off Irish whiskey," he announced to loud cheers from the crowd.

He also weighed in on the growing controversy over AI safety, saying that "negative" forces opposed its development.

On Saturday, he caught his Irish hosts and neighbouring Britain off-guard when he announced he would "love to see" a united Ireland.

Breaking with Washington's traditional neutrality on the historically charged topic, Trump argued that reunification of the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland — after more than a century apart — was "going to happen eventually".

"It may as well happen now," he said as he met Ireland's Prime Minister Micheal Martin in Dublin, prompting pushback from British loyalists in Northern Ireland and some leading UK politicians.

But he reaffirmed his remarks Sunday.

"It would seem to me that one of the naturals of all time is to put them together," he added, insisting "many people agree".

Trump's arrival in Doonbeg on Saturday sparked road closures and police checkpoints. Around 30 people protested his visit in Doonbeg village on Sunday.

"Donald Trump is not welcome in Ireland," William Hederman, 53, told the Agence France-Presse (AFP) news agency, accusing him of helping Israel commit genocide in Gaza.

Trump's attendance at the golf course he has owned since 2014 added extra complexity to a security effort reportedly costing Ireland €20 million ($32.4 million).

The former real estate magnate, who promotes his enterprises at every opportunity, was joined in the remote corner of Ireland by his sons Eric and Don Jr.

They have managed the family business since their 80-year-old father returned to the White House last year.

The course — set among dunes on the rugged County Clare coastline — has twice been targeted by pro-Palestinian activists in the past 18 months.

Police said three women — aged in their 20s, 30s and 40s — had appeared in a western Irish court late Saturday after being arrested for separate trespass and public order offences there.

Around 4,000 Irish and US security personnel were involved in the weekend security operation, with anti-drone technology among the measures deployed.

The president plays golf most weekends at one of his family's US properties. He is scheduled to host December's G20 summit at his Miami golfing resort.

Opposition Democrats have long complained that blurring the lines between his presidency and personal business interests is corrupt.

The White House has aggressively pushed back against claims that Trump has used his presidency to enrich himself, as his personal wealth has rocketed during his second term.

"Since the Civil War, we haven't had a president with a significant financial conflict of interest from a business enterprise," University of Minnesota Law School professor Richard Painter told AFP.

The former White House ethics lawyer warned Trump's conduct could send the message "that the way to curry a favour with the president is to patronise his properties, do business with his companies and so forth".

title: Why Australia's richest suburbs could be a warning for every homeowner
text:
IN BRIEF Upper-quartile home prices in two Australian capital cities have fallen at more than double the rate of entry-level housing.

Rising borrowing costs are forcing buyers toward cheaper stock, leaving luxury listings vulnerable to widening discounts.

Across Australia's capital cities, prices in the upper end of the property market are dropping rapidly, with experts warning it could indicate where the rest of the sector is headed.

Recent data from property analytics firm Cotality reveals that upper-quartile house prices — those in the top 25 per cent — have fallen at more than double the rate of entry-level ones in Sydney and Melbourne.

High-end homes in both cities have seen declines of more than 10 per cent in value from their peak. By contrast, those in the lower quartile have seen declines of just 3.9 to 5.4 per cent.

In Sydney, a mansion in Balmain East sold for an extraordinary $7 million loss this month — after selling for almost $20 million in 2022, it was bought for $12.8 million.

Cotality executive research director Tim Lawless told SBS News that the top end of the housing market historically moves first in a property cycle. While the sector overall peaked in March, the upper end peaked in October/November last year.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

As the Reserve Bank's rate hikes filter through, Lawless said buyers are being hit with a severe credit crunch as borrowing rates hover around 9.5 per cent, severely weakening purchasing power.

A household on a median income is now spending more than 50 per cent of its pre-tax income to serve a median-priced mortgage. As a result, those who might have previously looked in the middle-to-upper bracket are being pushed toward cheaper stock.

"Mainstream demand is getting deflected towards lower price points where buyers can actually demonstrate an ability to service the loan," Lawless explained.

Taken together, first home buyers, investors, and price-sensitive mid-tier individuals are all now competing for limited stock, which has left high-end listings exposed.

No urgency on the auction floor

The impact of the demand vacuum at the top has been visible on the ground for some time, with vendor discounting widening while time-on-the-market has lengthened.

Director and chief auctioneer at New South Wales independent AuctionWorks noted that the sharpest initial repricing has likely passed, however wealthy buyers are in no rush to step back in.

Broad market activity has cooled alongside price drops, with Cotality data showing capital city auction volumes down 31.1 per cent compared to the same period last year. Source: Getty / Bloomberg

"The top end of the market has been the most affected, with significant price adjustments occurring in recent months," Davidson told SBS News.

"However, it appears that whilst we may not yet have seen the bottom of the market, the price reductions have certainly slowed."

Davidson added that buyers are beginning to recognise value, but a lack of urgency remains the defining feature of higher-end auctions at present.

"Buyers are starting to see some value, however, there is no urgency to jump in just yet," he said. "This will change in the months ahead when price reductions slow even further."

Political debate continues

The widening property slump has sparked a fierce political debate over what is driving the correction.

Opposition leader Angus Taylor and senior Coalition MPs have blamed the government's recent tax adjustments including negative gearing, saying market confidence has been "smashed".

Opposition treasury spokesperson Tim Wilson says the housing correction "doesn't help" anyone, as first-home buyers are forced to spend more while those who own their own homes see their wealth decline.

READ MORE Death of the auction? Sellers move to private sales in softening market

Labor leaders have strongly rejected such framing, with Treasurer Jim Chalmers pointing to Treasury modelling showing that tax changes only account for a minor fraction of the shift. He attributes the downturn to high debt levels and elevated interest rates.

Housing minister Clare O'Neil maintained that top-down adjustments are a standard feature of property cycles and pointed to softening market values as a necessary step toward restoring access for first-home buyers.

In the two decades to 2021, CoreLogic data shows the median house price in Australia increased more than sixfold, rising from $123,000 to $795,000.

The domino effect

While the top end has absorbed the initial blow, Cotality's latest figures indicate that the bottom end is starting to come down as well.

Transaction volumes have declined by more than 15 per cent nationwide as listings increase across capital cities.

"Lower-priced housing is no longer insulated," Lawless said, noting that the gap between top and bottom price changes is narrowing as broader economic headwinds take hold.

With higher-end price falls tapering off, the top-end is expected to continue to dictate the future of the market at large with the cheaper credit that fuelled price rises now vanishing.

title: 'Living in an online world': Why this state is cutting back on classroom screen time
text:
in brief New South Wales will enforce daily caps on student screen time starting in 2027 to address falling test scores.

Under the policy, daily device use for kindergarten through year 2 will be limited to 15 minutes.

Students will be forced back to pen and paper as a state government moves to cap daily screen time to as little as 15 minutes against a backdrop of falling test scores.

New South Wales public schools will introduce daily screen-time limits for the start of the 2027 classroom year before the changes become mandatory from 2028 to allow time for teachers to make adjustments.

It follows similar moves from the Victorian government to reduce screen time in the classroom from 2027.

NSW Education Minister Prue Car said government research showed excessive screen use was a problem.

"An entire generation of students are increasingly living in an online world," she said on Sunday.

"We have a responsibility to ensure their health and education isn't adversely affected by excessive screen use.

"When the research is telling us teenagers are spending as much as seven hours a day on screens and we are seeing reading and writing skills going backwards for a whole generation of children, we have to act."

Schools are advised to limit screen-based homework, with the use of digital devices not recommended before Year 5.

NSW public schools will cap daily classroom screen time for young students as part of a push to return to pen-and-paper learning. Source: AAP / Marcus Brandt/dpa/picture-alliance/Sipa USA

New state guidelines also recommend at least an hour daily of pen-and-paper learning, citing benefits of handwriting and reading print.

The move follows OECD Programme for International Student Assessment exam results showing Australian high school students registering record-low scores in mathematics and reading.

Australian students spend nearly twice as long using digital devices for learning compared to the OECD average.

Recent National Assessment Program Literacy and Numeracy results mirrored the findings.

About a third of students failed to meet basic benchmarks; reading scores dropped across all grades compared to the previous year, and only Year 5 students showed writing improvement.

New policies to support healthy development

Under the NSW policy, daily screen time limits — averaged across a school week — will be set at 15 minutes for kindergarten to Year 2, 30 minutes for Years 3–4 and 45 minutes for Years 5–6.

High school students are capped at one-quarter of class time per subject in Years 7–10 and up to half in Years 11–12.

READ MORE The countries showing Australia a way out of its 'miserable' classroom situation

There will be exemptions and adjustments for students with disability, those with additional needs, or students for whom English is not their first language, or where digital support is part of a personalised learning plan.

NSW Health chief paediatrician Helen Goodwin said it was important to limit screen time for children.

"A healthy day for children and young people includes a mix of being active, getting enough sleep, and building active social connections with their peers and family," she said.

"We know that too much time spent on screens impacts these important daily activities that support healthy growth and development."

title: 'Proud to be a houso': Anthony Albanese condemns Hanson's remarks on late mother
text:
IN BRIEF One Nation leader Pauline Hanson criticised the time Albanese's mother spent in public housing.

Albanese told reporters on Sunday that his mother was "way out of Pauline Hanson's league".

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has criticised Pauline Hanson's comments about his late mother living in public housing for decades, saying he was proud of his upbringing and defending his mother as "way out of Pauline Hanson's league".

"She made comments about me being complaining about being growing up in public housing — nothing could be further from the truth," Albanese told reporters in Sydney on Sunday.

"I'm proud to be a houso and I'm proud of the community in which I grew up."

The comments follow resurfaced footage from Hanson's February appearance on a podcast, in which she mimicked Albanese crying while mocking his account of growing up in social housing in Sydney's inner west.

She argued Albanese's mother should not have remained in the same public housing property all her life.

What did Pauline Hanson say?

Appearing on The Karl Stefanovic Show in February, the One Nation leader was asked about Albanese. In response, she feigned tears while delivering a joke impression of the prime minister.

"Oh, I've actually grew up in a housing commission house. You have no idea how hard it is to grow up in a housing commission house. Oh, my God... talk about a Prime Minister," Hanson said on the podcast.

Hanson added that she had grown up on a street with housing commission homes and that the people who lived in them "had jobs, they worked".

"He said his mother lived in the same one she was born in for 65 years. Sorry, that's not on, to me," she continued.

"It should be a limited time — you've been given a hand up, move it on to the next ones coming through."

On Friday, she doubled down on those comments, telling The Australian the prime minister "complains about his housing commission upbringing".

She also questioned Albanese's account compared to Australians "being forced to live in cars and tents" because of what she called "his government's high immigration numbers".

'Way out of Pauline Hanson's league'

Albanese's mother, Maryanne, was a single mother and disability pensioner who lived with chronic rheumatoid arthritis for most of her adult life.

She died in 2002, aged 65, having spent decades in the same public housing property where Albanese also grew up.

Albanese gave an extended account of her life on Sunday morning, describing a woman who worked cleaning offices overnight to support him and who was left barely able to hold a knife and fork as her arthritis worsened.

Albanese was born to a single mum, Maryanne, in council housing. Credit: Office of Anthony Albanese

"She was compassionate, not uncaring. She was generous, not mean. And she was kind, not nasty," Albanese said.

"She was a person of great character. She had a tough life … [but] she never complained. She never denigrated anyone.

"I grew up in a community that looked after each other. It was the opposite of being elite."

READ MORE Anthony Albanese promises to unite Australia with vision of optimism as new prime minister

Albanese said he hadn't seen the comments when they first aired, but was "stunned" to see them when they resurfaced.

"She was a battler, and for Pauline Hanson to attack someone and their character — who died in 2002, some 24 years ago, at age just 65 — because she did have such a tough life with her health from an early age," he said.

"I am stunned at these comments, but I'll make this point: if Pauline Hanson wants to criticise me, then that's fine. But my mother was way out of Pauline Hanson's league."

Condemnation across the board

Hanson's remarks drew criticism from both sides of politics.

Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie — who is currently locked in a separate, escalating dispute with Hanson after she posted a cartoon labelling him a "traitor" over his testimony in the Ben Roberts-Smith defamation case — said the comments were another sign she was unfit for office.

"Let's leave mums out of it," he told News24 on Sunday. "This is another indicator to the Australian people that she's not fit to be prime minister."

Trade Minister Don Farrell called the remarks "appalling".

"Anthony loves his mother … to have them attacked publicly in this way is just appalling," Farrell told News24 on Sunday.

"There's a certain bitterness in One Nation’s approach to the world that I find quite un-Australian actually."

He said that if she wanted "dignity and respect" from those in politics, an apology was necessary.

"Attacking the prime minister's mother like this is not a way to get respect and dignity from your colleagues," he said.

On Saturday, Energy Minister Chris Bowen said: "attacking a woman who has been dead for more than 20 years for living in public housing is off-limits".

"We can have a debate between politicians – leave families alone, particularly a family member who's deceased. For God's sake, there's a line — and Pauline Hanson regularly crosses the line."

title: 'It could take over the entire internet': The threat top tech leaders say could arise in a year
text:
in brief Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called on tech firms to slow down frontier AI development.

Rivals Sam Altman and Elon Musk backed the proposal amid growing AI safety concerns.

The boss of one of the world's major artificial intelligence companies has called for an urgent slowdown in development amid mounting fears over the risks of "superintelligent" computer systems and its threat to humanity.

The intervention came after a former employee at Anthropic, which is behind the Claude AI chatbot, warned that AI could kill off humanity in a few years' time.

The company's chief executive Dario Amodei on Sunday (AEST) said he was concerned by AI's ability to self-improve could outrun humanity's ability to control it, and by a recent incident in which rogue AI agents attacked targets they were not asked to.

He offered three-step plan intended to pace development and create more time to manage its risks.

In a lengthy essay shared on X he said: "We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain".

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"Not building the technology deprives humanity of benefits or simply places AI in the hands of authoritarian powers, while building it too fast is reckless," he added. "We have sought a middle way."

"But over the last few months, I have become convinced that fully addressing the risks requires even more prudence."

His company's competitors agreed. Both Elon Musk, who runs xAI, and Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, quickly chimed in on the social media platform to express agreement with Amodei's assessment.

"Dario is right," Musk wrote, while Altman posted: "Committing to having independent evaluators with employee-like access is a great idea, and we will do the same," adding that more information would be shared soon.

Rogue agents and security risks

Amodei made his essay public after San Francisco-based Anthropic released a threat intelligence report on Thursday detailing how several actors had used its Claude AI models for activities ranging from weapons development and cyber operations to surveillance and fraud.

Amodei pointed to AI's growing ability to improve itself, highlighting long-held concerns about it outpacing human ability to control its operation, along with the recent incident involving OpenAI and Hugging Face as his primary reasons to put the brakes on model advances.

Alarm about the potential harm from AI grew this week when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned, accusing both US tech giants of "gambling with our lives" in the race toward superintelligence.

READ MORE AI escaped its testing sandbox and hacked a website. The law is still catching up

Coxon, 27, who previously worked at OpenAI before joining Anthropic, stated that "the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade".

Anthropic has positioned itself as the more safety-conscious frontier lab, but is not immune to these concerns.

Last week it disclosed another instance of an AI model hacking external systems, after a July incident in which some of its Claude models had hacked into the systems of three companies during cybersecurity tests.

The Reuters news agency reported last week that a swarm of rogue OpenAI agents hijacked a German website and transformed it into a bulletin board for other AI agents.

The plan to slow AI's uncontrolled growth

Amodei cautioned that the Hugging Face breach should not be dismissed as a one-off.

"A swarm of agents essentially acted as a fanatically devoted collective, conducting cybersecurity attacks on targets they were not asked to attack," he explained.

"Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it's my worry that in 6-12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet, potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage."

As part of his proposed framework, Amodei called for embedded independent evaluators with employee-like access to verify safety practices, coordination among frontier AI firms to set safety standards, and international cooperation to manage AI risks.

He noted that a coordinated approach would enable leading US AI companies to carry out necessary safety research without putting themselves at a competitive disadvantage, likely requiring targeted antitrust exemptions in the United States.

However, Amodei emphasized that any slowdown by democratically governed countries should be limited to preserving the lead US AI firms hold over China.

"Pacing within democracies will be limited by the lead that US companies have over authoritarian regimes, chiefly the Chinese Communist Party," Amodei wrote, calling for tighter controls on advanced AI chips, model distillation, and theft of model weights.

There is also an enormous amount of money riding on staying ahead, as both OpenAI and Anthropic prepare for blockbuster initial public offerings.

Still, Amodei insisted he is not calling for halting technical progress altogether, but ensuring companies take adequate time to align and safeguard their models before deployment.

The impressive hit headlined the latest 61-hole batch of assays from the company’s 2026 resource upgrade and expansion drilling program. McLaren Minerals has hit an impressive 24 metres at 7.54 per cent heavy minerals at its wholly-owned McLaren titanium project in Western Australia. SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘We are all devastated’: Old Xavs apologise after administrative failure costs grand final berth Marc McGowan Updated September 15, 2026 — 1:20pm ,first published September 14, 2026 — 3:10pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The president of a powerhouse Victorian amateur football club forced to forfeit a grand final spot has taken full responsibility for selecting an ineligible player. Old Xaverians’ under-19 premier men’s team won its preliminary final over St Kevin’s on Saturday, but won’t contest the grand final against Old Brighton after a league investigation. Old Xavs have been booted from the VAFA under-19s premier grand final for fielding an ineligible player. Photo © Ari Hatzis The Victorian Amateur Football Association announced late on Sunday night that the Old Xavs would receive a $100 fine and forfeit their five-point victory over St Kevin’s for breaking finals eligibility rules. St Kevin’s, not Old Xaverians, will compete in this weekend’s grand final. This masthead is not suggesting that Old Xavs intended to break VAFA rules.

Advertisement

VAFA rules state that under-19s footballers cannot have played more than 12 games in the season in question in the Talent League – the AFL’s premier junior feeder competition – to retain finals eligibility. The player in question, who was on Oakleigh Chargers’ list and in Greater Western Sydney’s academy this season, exceeded that tally, but met other eligibility criteria, which required him to play at least five games for Old Xavs, including a minimum of two after June 30. This masthead contacted Old Xaverians president Michael Logan, general manager James Woods and under-19 coach Matthew Handley. In a statement on the club’s website, Logan said no one at Old Xavs intended to “deceive or act dishonestly”.

Advertisement

“We accept full responsibility for this error, as VAFA rules state that clubs are accountable for ensuring players’ final eligibility,” Logan wrote. “When the matter was brought to our attention, the club undertook a thorough review of the facts and circumstances surrounding the situation, including grounds for review. “At the conclusion of that review, we made submissions to the VAFA. Upon their further investigations, the VAFA’s position was that the ineligibility decision stood. We accept that position.” Logan said Old Xaverians had protocols in place to manage player eligibility, but that they had “failed” in this instance, so the club would review and strengthen the process to try to avoid this happening again. “The situation was in no way the fault of the player ruled ineligible,” he said.

Advertisement

“The club accepts responsibility for his being in this situation and I know he has received – and appreciates – the full support of his teammates. The way both he and his family have conducted themselves during this matter is a credit to them. “Equally, to the rest of the playing group and their families, the club apologises unreservedly. “We are all devastated that the season has ended like this. We have been greatly heartened by the care and support they have shown one another during a really difficult time.” St Kevin’s president Patrick Mount told this masthead on Monday it was an “unfortunate situation”, but that people at his club flagged the player’s ineligibility with the league once they noticed he played in the game. “There have been people saying we knew about it and kept it deliberately quiet, but team sheets can be changed until the last minute, and you don’t know if a player is actually going to play until you see them on the field,” Mount said.

Advertisement

“I didn’t know who he was personally, but we had a number of people on our side who flagged it, and every player’s profile on PlayHQ is publicly accessible and clearly showed he played 16 games in the Talent League. “The rule is black and white – you can’t play more than 12 [Talent League] games. “We have great respect for them as a football club, they have very good people in charge, and I don’t think this was anything more than an administrative oversight. I don’t think it was a deliberately sinister ploy to seek an unfair advantage.” In a statement, the VAFA said it had investigated and confirmed that Old Xaverians’ under-19 men’s team fielded an ineligible player against St Kevin’s on Saturday. “In accordance with VAFA rule 50, ‘A club which includes a player who is not eligible in a team by which it is represented in a premiership match shall be fined as prescribed in schedule of fines contained in rule 129 ($100) and shall forfeit all matches in which such player played … each such match shall be awarded to the opposing club...’,” the statement read.

Broken Hill Gold has launched a major geophysics program and is mobilising a second drill rig to its 100 per cent-owned White Dam gold-copper project in South Australia, ramping up the hunt for sulphides to determine whether its high-grade Icebreaker discovery is the tip of a much bigger iceberg. The company has started 48 line-kilometres of induced polarisation (IP) and 670 line-kilometres of high-resolution ground magnetics to pinpoint deeper sulphide targets. The surveys are due to be completed by mid-October, with initial results expected then. Broken Hill Gold’s induced polarisation geophysics survey is underway at its White Dam gold-copper project in South Australia. Icebreaker sits in the central White Dam project area, 80km west of Broken Hill, where historical exploration overwhelmingly chased shallow oxide gold suited to heap leaching. Broken Hill Gold struck paydirt, unearthing primary sulphides during ongoing oxide resource drilling and opening a new front beneath ground barely tested by previous explorers. Initial drilling returned a 20-metre hit at 2.5 grams per tonne (g/t) gold and 0.5 per cent copper from 58m, including 6m at 7.5g/t gold and 1.2 per cent copper from 66m. Later work delivered 46m at 1.1g/t gold and 0.3 per cent copper from 37m. Adding to the intrigue, Icebreaker sits within a magnetic anomaly extending for up to 1km and the company has reported the discovery open in all directions.

Advertisement

‘We anticipate the surveys being instrumental in defining clear, high-priority targets at depth, by mid-October.’ Broken Hill Gold managing director Matthew Boyes Broken Hill Gold sees deeper potential beyond Icebreaker. One particular deep hole beneath the nearby historical Hannaford pit returned 29m at 0.7g/t gold from 315m, adding weight to the company’s view that mineralisation beneath Hannaford and Vertigo remains open along strike and down dip. Broken Hill Gold managing director Matthew Boyes said: “Given the mineralisation styles observed in initial drilling, we anticipate the Induced Polarisation and high-resolution ground magnetic surveys being instrumental in defining clear, high-priority targets at depth, with initial results expected by mid-October.” The next phase takes the hunt deeper. A dedicated diamond rig is mobilising to work alongside the current reverse circulation (RC) oxide program, with drilling planned into the Icebreaker sulphide zone and beneath Vertigo and Hannaford. Diamond core will also retrieve sulphide material from Icebreaker andoxide mineralisation at Vertigo for metallurgical testwork, helping assess how the different ore styles could respond to processing as White Dam chases resource growth and moves towards an open-pit restart.

Advertisement

The two-rig setup forms part of an 18-month exploration push already underway, comprising more than 30,000m of RC and diamond drilling, electrical and magnetic geophysics and geochemistry across White Dam and regional targets including Wadnaminga. The work is expected to define and upgrade the resource. In parallel, September oxide drilling at Vertigo North Extended and Hannaford is expected to feed an updated and upgraded resource estimate in the fourth quarter, followed by open-pit optimisation and mine planning. Its Rolling, Hannaford East and Icebreaker targets are also in the near-mine oxide push to restart mining. Beyond the central mine area, Broken Hill is spreading its geophysical net across more than 50 underexplored historical prospects, where key targets were generally drilled no deeper than 80m. Survey coverage extends from nearby Vertigo and White Dam East to Mary Mine, 12km west of the White Dam mine, Wilkins 12km south and Green & Gold 16km southwest. There is plenty of historical smoke to chase. Mary Mine returned 16m at 0.9g/t gold and 2.2 per cent copper, while Green & Gold yielded 36m at 1g/t gold and 0.3 per cent copper. The company acquired White Dam in late 2025, inheriting an operation that previously produced 180,000 ounces. The project benefits from historical pits, heap-leach infrastructure and a gold extraction plant, which is expected to generate the cash to bankroll a broader exploration push.

The wider geological address adds another layer. White Dam sits in the Curnamona Province, which has already demonstrated its capacity to host large copper-gold deposits. Kalkaroo, 40km north, hosts 1.1 million tonnes of copper and 3.1 million ounces of gold. With geophysical crews mapping the subsurface and a second rig poised to punch deeper holes, Broken Hill Gold has two prizes in its sights: push White Dam’s oxide resources towards an open-pit restart while the surveys and drill bit determine whether Icebreaker has exposed the first glimpse of something much bigger underneath. The Ilksan prospect forms part of the broader Baynazar copper exploration project,just 25km south-west of Sarytogan’s world-class graphite deposit.
